Action hooks::useActionState.summary: useActionState connects a form action to its latest returned state and pending status. It also supplies a wrapped action for form or button submission.
Action hooks::useActionState.explanation: Call useActionState at the top level with an action and initial state. It returns the latest action result, a form-compatible action, and a pending flag; the wrapped action receives previous state before the submitted payload.
Action hooks::useActionState.syntax: const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(fn, initialState, permalink?);

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Function called when the form is submitted or a button is pressed; it receives the previous state followed by the action payload.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: Initial value of the returned state before the action has been invoked.

parameters.name: permalink
parameters.description: Optional unique page URL for progressive enhancement with React Server Components.

Action hooks::useActionState.returns: An array of [state, formAction, isPending]: the current result state, a wrapped action for form action or formAction props, and a flag indicating whether a Transition is pending.

example.title: Form action with result and pending UI
example.explanation: The action receives the previous state and submitted FormData, then returns the next state displayed by the component.

useCases.title: Show the latest action result
useCases.scenario: Display validation or server feedback after a form submission.

useCases.title: Provide pending feedback
useCases.scenario: Disable controls and show a progress label while an async action runs.

useCases.title: Preserve submissions across hydration
useCases.scenario: Support progressive enhancement for forms backed by Server Functions.

interview.question: What does useActionState return?
interview.answer: It returns an array containing the current state, a wrapped action, and isPending. The state starts as initialState and becomes the action's returned value after invocation.
interview.followUp: What does the wrapped action do? It can be supplied to a form's action prop or a button's formAction prop, and it may also be called manually inside startTransition.

interview.question: What arguments does the action receive?
interview.answer: The action receives the previous state first, followed by the submitted action payload. For a form submission, that payload is typically FormData.
interview.followUp: Why is previous state useful? It lets the action validate or update from the last result rather than reconstructing that state elsewhere.

interview.question: How should pending state be used?
interview.answer: isPending indicates whether a Transition associated with this hook is pending. It can drive disabled controls or progress feedback while the action runs.
interview.followUp: How can a form work before hydration with a Server Function? A permalink can provide the page URL for progressive enhancement, while React replays the submission after hydration.

keyPoints: Invoke the Hook at component top level; it manages state updated by a form action.
The state represents the most recent action result, not merely input values.
Before any submission, the returned state equals the supplied initialState.
Use the returned action directly on a form or as a button's formAction.
Use isPending to render progress feedback or prevent duplicate interaction.
The Hook wraps an existing action rather than replacing the action's business logic.
gotchas: When invoking the returned action outside a form, call it within startTransition.
The action's first parameter is previous state, so its signature differs from an ordinary form action.

Action hooks::useActionState server acti.summary: useActionState connects an Action to component state, making the latest result available to render. With a Server Function, it can expose server-side validation results before hydration and optionally support progressive enhancement.
Action hooks::useActionState server acti.explanation: Place useActionState at the top level of a Client Component, passing an action and initial state. React calls the action with the previous state followed by the submitted payload; the hook returns the latest result, a wrapped action for the form, and a pending flag. With a Server Function, the result can appear before hydration, and permalink enables progressive enhancement for dynamic pages.
Action hooks::useActionState server acti.syntax: const [state, dispatchAction, isPending] = useActionState(reducerAction, initialState, permalink?);

parameters.name: reducerAction
parameters.description: Function invoked by the Action. It receives previous state first, then the payload passed to the returned dispatch action.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: Initial value of the state, used during the first render.

parameters.name: permalink
parameters.description: Optional unique URL for the page modified by the form; used for progressive enhancement with Server Functions.

Action hooks::useActionState server acti.returns: An array containing the current state, a dispatch action, and an isPending boolean.

example.title: Display server-style validation state
example.explanation: The returned action receives the form submission, while the returned state displays the latest validation result.

useCases.title: Server-side validation feedback
useCases.scenario: A form submits invalid data and the server returns field or form errors for rendering.

useCases.title: Progressive enhancement
useCases.scenario: A form must remain usable before the client bundle finishes loading.

useCases.title: Pending submission state
useCases.scenario: The UI should disable controls while an asynchronous submission is running.

interview.question: What does useActionState return and how are its arguments ordered?
interview.answer: useActionState takes an action, an initial state, and optionally a permalink. It returns the current state, a wrapped dispatch action, and whether that action is pending. The action receives previous state first, then the payload.
interview.followUp: Why is previous state first? The hook is designed to derive each result from the prior result, while the second argument carries the submitted form data or other payload.

interview.question: How does useActionState support server-side validation?
interview.answer: A Server Function can be passed to useActionState in a Client Component and connected to a form. React can then show the server response before hydration completes, so returned validation data can be rendered immediately.
interview.followUp: What enables submission before JavaScript loads? A Server Function used as the form action, plus an appropriate permalink when the page has dynamic content.

interview.question: What is permalink for?
interview.answer: The optional permalink is the unique URL for the page the form modifies. If a Server Function form submits before the JavaScript bundle loads, the browser navigates there instead of the current URL.
interview.followUp: When can permalink be omitted? Omit it when the current URL is sufficient or the page does not need progressive enhancement for dynamic content.

keyPoints: It tracks the result of an Action and exposes that result as component state.
Call the hook at the component’s top level, not inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
The reducerAction runs when the wrapped action is invoked.
The action receives the previous state as its first argument, followed by the submitted payload.
Use the returned dispatch function as a form action or from another Action.
Server Functions let the latest server result render before client hydration finishes.
A permalink supports submissions on dynamic pages before JavaScript is available.
gotchas: Call the returned dispatch function only from an Action, such as a form action or a function wrapped in startTransition.

Action hooks::useFormStatus.summary: Reads the submission status of a parent form from a component nested inside it. Use its pending value to show progress or disable submit controls while the form action runs.
Action hooks::useFormStatus.explanation: useFormStatus lets a component rendered inside a form observe the nearest parent form's submission status without receiving status props. Read pending for in-flight submission state, or inspect data, method, and action for details about the active parent submission.
Action hooks::useFormStatus.syntax: const { pending, data, method, action } = useFormStatus();
Action hooks::useFormStatus.returns: A status object containing pending, data, method, and action.

example.title: Disable a submit button while the form action runs
example.explanation: A nested submit button reads the parent form's pending state and disables itself while the action runs.

useCases.title: Disable or relabel a submit button
useCases.scenario: A form action is submitting

useCases.title: Display the active FormData
useCases.scenario: Submitted fields need immediate feedback

useCases.title: Build nested form-aware controls
useCases.scenario: A reusable control needs form context

interview.question: What does useFormStatus return?
interview.answer: It returns a status object describing the last submission of the parent form. Its fields are pending, data, method, and action; pending indicates whether that parent form is actively submitting.
interview.followUp: What happens if the Hook is used in a component outside a form? The Hook cannot read a parent form, so status fields that depend on one have no parent-form status; place the component inside the form.

interview.question: Where must useFormStatus be called?
interview.answer: The component calling useFormStatus must be rendered inside the form whose status it needs. This makes a nested submit control able to disable itself while the parent form action is pending.
interview.followUp: Why can’t the form-rendering component use the Hook for its own form? The Hook reads a parent form, not a form rendered by that same component.

interview.question: How do the status fields differ?
interview.answer: pending is true while the parent form is pending submission and false otherwise. data contains the submitted FormData during an active submission, method is get or post, and action references the parent form’s action function.
interview.followUp: When is data null? It is null when there is no active submission or no parent form.

keyPoints: Use it to read information about the parent form’s most recent submission.
Use pending to render loading feedback or disable a nested submit control during submission.
The returned object exposes pending, data, method, and action.
pending becomes true while the parent form is submitting.
data represents the parent form’s submitted fields as FormData while an active submission exists.
method identifies whether the parent form submits with GET or POST.
gotchas: Call the Hook in a descendant component, not directly in the component that renders the form.
The Hook reports only the parent form; it does not observe a form rendered by the same component or a descendant.
The data field is null when submission is idle or when no parent form exists.

Action hooks::useOptimistic.summary: `useOptimistic` temporarily shows an anticipated state while an Action is pending. Once the Action finishes or fails, the UI returns to the Hook's base value.
Action hooks::useOptimistic.explanation: The Hook returns a temporary state plus a setter for an Action. Calling the setter during a pending Action makes React render that anticipated value; after the Action finishes or fails, the Hook falls back to the value supplied to the Hook.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The ordinary state value used outside a pending Action and after the Action finishes.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Optional function receiving the current pending state and the setter's input, returning the next optimistic state.

Action hooks::useOptimistic.returns: An array containing `optimisticState`, the currently displayed temporary or base state, and `set`, the function for requesting an optimistic value inside an Action.

example.title: Optimistic like count
example.explanation: The button shows the anticipated count during the Action, then the real state becomes authoritative when the asynchronous work completes.

useCases.title: Optimistic form submission
useCases.scenario: Show a submitted message immediately with a pending label while a network request runs.

useCases.title: Responsive data updates
useCases.scenario: Render the expected result of a mutation before the server confirms it.

useCases.title: Instant feedback
useCases.scenario: Display an anticipated counter or status during an asynchronous Action.

interview.question: What does useOptimistic return?
interview.answer: `useOptimistic(value, reducer?)` returns `[optimisticState, set]`. The first item is normally `value`, but while an Action is pending it is the reducer result, or the value passed to the setter when no reducer exists.
interview.followUp: What happens after the Action errors? React returns to the `value` supplied to the Hook, so the optimistic display does not become the committed state automatically.

interview.question: When may the optimistic setter be called?
interview.answer: The setter must run inside an Action. React then re-renders immediately with the anticipated result while the Action is pending.
interview.followUp: How can a component establish the required Action boundary? Use an async transition with `startTransition`, unless the update already runs in another supported Action context.

interview.question: How does the base value relate to the optimistic state?
interview.answer: The `value` argument is the non-optimistic source of truth. It determines what React displays after the Action completes, and it is shown whenever no Action is in progress.
interview.followUp: Why should the Action update the real state as well? The optimistic setter is temporary; the underlying value must be updated when the operation succeeds so the final render reflects committed data.

keyPoints: Invoke the Hook at component top level, not conditionally or inside an event handler.
The returned state normally mirrors the base value and diverges only during a pending Action.
With a reducer, React derives the temporary state from pending state and the setter input; without one, the setter input is used directly.
An in-Action setter call immediately refreshes the UI with the anticipated state.
The Hook's first argument controls the post-Action display and acts as the committed fallback.
The optimistic value may use any data type, provided it matches the component's state model.
gotchas: Call the setter only from an Action. Calling it elsewhere causes a warning and the optimistic value may render only briefly.
If the surrounding code is not already an Action, wrap the optimistic update in `startTransition`.
Do not treat the optimistic value as durable state; the base `value` is displayed outside the pending Action.

Action hooks::useOptimistic rollback.summary: useOptimistic shows a temporary state during an async Action. If the Action fails and the source value was not committed, React renders that unchanged source value again, automatically rolling back the optimistic UI.
Action hooks::useOptimistic rollback.explanation: useOptimistic displays a temporary state only while an Action is pending. When the Action fails, React renders the current source value again; because the source is normally changed only after success, the optimistic change disappears automatically.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The current source-of-truth state used when no Action is pending and after the optimistic period ends.

parameters.name: updateFn
parameters.description: Receives the current state and the Action's input, returning the temporary state shown while the Action is pending.

Action hooks::useOptimistic rollback.returns: A pair containing the optimistic state and a function that applies an optimistic update: `[optimisticState, addOptimistic]`. The optimistic state equals the source value unless an Action is pending.

example.title: Rollback an optimistic message
example.explanation: The form Action adds a temporary message immediately. If saving succeeds, the source state is updated; if it fails, the unchanged source state is rendered again, removing the optimistic message.

useCases.title: Instant mutation feedback
useCases.scenario: A network mutation is pending and the interface should immediately reflect the expected result.

useCases.title: Failed deletion rollback
useCases.scenario: A delete Action fails and the item should reappear without manually restoring a snapshot.

useCases.title: Responsive form submission
useCases.scenario: A form submission should show pending content while the server request runs.

interview.question: How does `useOptimistic` roll back after a failed Action?
interview.answer: `useOptimistic` receives the source state and returns an optimistic value plus a setter. The setter schedules a temporary value through its update function while an Action is pending; outside that period, the source value is returned.
interview.followUp: What causes rollback? When the Action completes or throws, the pending optimistic state ends and React renders the current source value. If the source changed only after success, the failed update disappears.

interview.question: Where should the optimistic setter be called?
interview.answer: The setter must run inside an Action, such as a function passed to a form's `action` prop. React then associates the optimistic render with the pending transition and removes it when that Action ends.
interview.followUp: What happens if the setter is called outside an Action? React warns, and the optimistic state can render only briefly rather than being tracked for the Action's lifetime.

interview.question: What role does the `value` argument play in rollback?
interview.answer: The `value` argument is the source of truth after the Action finishes. On success, update that source from the confirmed result; on failure, leave it unchanged so React displays the pre-update state again.
interview.followUp: How should an application report failure? Catch the Action's error and show an error message while allowing the unchanged source state to provide the rollback.

keyPoints: Calling the setter during an Action causes an immediate render of the temporary optimistic state.
Outside a pending Action, the hook exposes the supplied source value rather than an old optimistic snapshot.
React converges the optimistic and source values without requiring a separate clearing state update.
When the Action finishes, the temporary and real states are reconciled in one render.
The first argument determines the post-Action display, so successful source updates must be reflected there.
A failed mutation rolls back naturally when the parent leaves the source value unchanged.
gotchas: Call the optimistic setter inside an Action, such as a form action; otherwise React warns and may render the temporary state only briefly.
Rollback does not restore an independently changed source value; React re-renders whatever source state currently exists when the Action ends.
Automatic rollback does not provide user-facing error handling, so catch the failed Action when the interface should explain what happened.

Async hooks::use.summary: use reads a Promise or context during rendering. Promise reads coordinate with Suspense while pending and Error Boundaries when rejected.
Async hooks::use.explanation: During rendering, use reads a Promise's resolved value or a context value. A pending Promise suspends the component, allowing the nearest Suspense boundary to show its fallback; rejection is handled by the nearest Error Boundary. Unlike Hooks, use may appear in conditions and loops, but it must still receive the Promise itself.

parameters.name: promise
parameters.description: A Promise whose resolved value should be read; reuse the same cached instance across re-renders.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: A React context whose current value should be read.

Async hooks::use.returns: The resource value: the resolved Promise value or the current context value.

example.title: Read a Promise during rendering
example.explanation: The component reads a cached Promise during rendering; Suspense supplies fallback UI while the Promise is pending.

useCases.title: Render asynchronous data
useCases.scenario: A component receives a cached data Promise from a Suspense-enabled framework and needs its resolved value during render.

useCases.title: Conditional context access
useCases.scenario: A component must read context only after an early return or within a conditional branch.

useCases.title: Promise through context
useCases.scenario: A provider needs to share asynchronous data without threading it through every intermediate component.

interview.question: What does use do with a Promise?
interview.answer: use reads a resource during rendering. With a Promise, it returns the resolved value and suspends the component while the Promise is pending; Suspense can then render a fallback.
interview.followUp: What happens if the Promise rejects? The nearest Error Boundary handles the rejection, rather than the Suspense fallback.

interview.question: How does use differ from useContext?
interview.answer: use can receive context and works similarly to useContext, returning the context's current value. Unlike useContext, it may be used inside conditions and loops.
interview.followUp: What constraint remains? The calling function must still be a component or Hook, even though use is not itself a Hook.

interview.question: Why must Promises passed to use be cached?
interview.answer: A Promise passed to use must be cached so the same instance is reused across renders. This lets React track its pending, fulfilled, or rejected state consistently.
interview.followUp: How can asynchronous data cross component boundaries? Put a cached Promise in context, read it with use(context), then resolve it with use(promise).

keyPoints: use reads a Promise or context resource while the component renders.
Unlike ordinary Hooks, use may be called conditionally or inside loops.
A pending Promise pauses the component's rendering until React can read its result.
Promise rejection is surfaced through the nearest Error Boundary.
After resolution, Suspense replaces its fallback with the component output using the value.
Passing context makes use return that context's value in the same general way as useContext.
gotchas: Do not create a new Promise during render; cache it so React receives the same Promise instance on every re-render.
Do not inspect Promise internals to bypass React's resource handling; pass the Promise to use instead.
Although use can be conditional, the call that reads a Promise must not be skipped or substituted after the Promise is chosen.

Async hooks::use with conditional contex.summary: React’s `use` can read context conditionally or inside loops, unlike `useContext`, which must be called at the component’s top level. It returns the value from the closest matching provider above the calling component.
Async hooks::use with conditional contex.explanation: Import `use` from React and pass it a context object during rendering. Unlike `useContext`, `use` may appear after an early return or inside an `if` or loop; React resolves the value from the closest provider above the calling component. The call must still be made from a component or Hook, and context should be passed directly to `use`.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: A React context object whose current value should be read during rendering.

Async hooks::use with conditional contex.returns: The context value supplied by the closest matching provider above the calling component.

example.title: Conditionally reading context
example.explanation: When show is true, the component reads the nearest ThemeContext provider; otherwise it returns without reading the context.

useCases.title: Read context after an early return
useCases.scenario: A component returns early for missing or invalid input, then needs context only for the main rendering path.

useCases.title: Branch-dependent context access
useCases.scenario: A feature flag or prop determines whether a component needs a theme, locale, or service context.

useCases.title: Iterate over context reads
useCases.scenario: A component processes multiple context objects or resources in an iteration.

interview.question: How does `use` differ from `useContext` for conditional context reads?
interview.answer: `use(Context)` reads the context value during rendering and returns the value from the closest matching provider above the component. It behaves like `useContext` for context reading, but it may be placed in a conditional or loop.
interview.followUp: Why can this help after an early return? `useContext` must be called at the component's top level, whereas `use` can be called only on the branch that needs the context.

interview.question: Can `use` read context inside an `if` statement?
interview.answer: Yes. A component can call `use(ThemeContext)` inside an `if` block, so it can avoid reading the context when the condition is false. The official example uses this pattern for conditional rendering of a horizontal rule.
interview.followUp: What must still be true? The call must execute during component or Hook rendering and must not be placed in `try`/`catch`.

interview.question: Which provider supplies the value returned by `use(Context)?
interview.answer: React resolves context by searching upward from the calling component and selecting the closest provider for the supplied context. If no nearer provider intervenes, the nearest available provider determines the value.
interview.followUp: What is the practical implication? Moving or inserting a provider above the component can change the value returned by `use(Context)`.

keyPoints: The React `use` API reads a resource during rendering; context is one supported resource type.
Use `use(Context)` when context access must occur in a branch or loop rather than at the component's top level.
The return value is the current value associated with the context argument.
Provider lookup is hierarchical: React chooses the closest matching provider above the component.
A conditional call lets a component read context only for the rendering path that needs it.
The lookup is relative to the component that performs the call, not to an arbitrary descendant.
gotchas: `use` may be conditional, but its Promise-specific rule still applies: call it for the Promise itself rather than inspecting Promise internals.
Do not place `use` inside `try`/`catch` blocks.
The call must remain inside a React component or custom Hook.

Async hooks::use with promises.summary: Read a stable Promise with use during rendering. React suspends while it is pending and uses Suspense or the nearest Error Boundary for pending or rejected states.
Async hooks::use with promises.explanation: Pass a cached Promise to a component and call use during rendering. React suspends that component while the Promise is pending, returns its fulfilled value afterward, and sends rejection handling to the nearest Error Boundary rather than a try/catch block.

parameters.name: promise
parameters.description: A Promise whose fulfilled value should be read; cache it so the same instance is reused across re-renders.

Async hooks::use with promises.returns: The fulfilled value read from the Promise.

example.title: Read a Promise with use
example.explanation: Pass a cached Promise into the component and call use during rendering; Suspense supplies temporary UI until the Promise fulfills.

useCases.title: Read asynchronous data
useCases.scenario: Render data supplied by a cached asynchronous resource.

useCases.title: Coordinate loading UI
useCases.scenario: Show a loading fallback while a resource is pending.

useCases.title: Handle asynchronous errors
useCases.scenario: Display a dedicated failure state when loading rejects.

interview.question: What happens when use receives a pending Promise?
interview.answer: use can read a Promise during rendering. While that Promise is pending, the component suspends and a surrounding Suspense boundary can show its fallback; after fulfillment, use returns the value.
interview.followUp: How should rejection be handled? Put the component using use inside an Error Boundary, whose fallback is shown if the Promise rejects.

interview.question: How does use handle a rejected Promise?
interview.answer: A rejected Promise is handled through the nearest Error Boundary, which displays its fallback. use itself is not placed in a try/catch block.
interview.followUp: What alternative can avoid an Error Boundary? Catch the Promise rejection and resolve it to another value before passing it to use.

interview.question: How is use different from other Hooks?
interview.answer: Unlike ordinary Hooks, use may appear inside conditions and loops. The calling function must still be a component or Hook, and use must run during rendering.
interview.followUp: What restriction remains despite conditional support? The call cannot be wrapped in try/catch, and its Promise must be cached across re-renders.

keyPoints: Calling use with a Promise gives the component its fulfilled result.
Pending work pauses the component until the Promise settles.
Promise identity must remain stable between renders.
gotchas: Do not create a new Promise during rendering; provide a cached instance so React can reuse it across re-renders.

Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue.summary: useDeferredValue lets a slow UI subtree update behind an urgent value, such as text input. React may keep the previous deferred value briefly while preparing the newer render in the background.
Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue.explanation: Call this Hook at component level to derive a deferred version of a value. When the value changes, React can render first with the previous deferred value and then retry the slower subtree in the background with the new value, allowing urgent UI such as an input to update sooner.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value whose updates should be deferred; it can be any type.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: Optional value returned during the component's initial render. Without it, the initial render is not deferred.

Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue.returns: Returns the current deferred value: initialValue or the supplied value on the first render, then potentially the previous value during an update before React produces the new value in a background render.

example.title: Keep input responsive while results lag
example.explanation: The input uses the immediate query, while Results receives a value that may temporarily remain behind it.

useCases.title: Responsive search
useCases.scenario: A controlled text field must remain responsive while filtering or rendering a large result list.

useCases.title: Defer expensive panels
useCases.scenario: A detail panel or results view is expensive to render and should catch up after navigation or selection changes.

useCases.title: Avoid abrupt loading replacement
useCases.scenario: A Suspense-enabled result view should keep showing previous content while new data becomes ready.

interview.question: What does useDeferredValue do?
interview.answer: It returns a deferred copy of the supplied value. On an update, React can first render with the previous copy and later attempt a background render with the new one, so urgent work can appear before a slow subtree catches up.
interview.followUp: How is it different from debouncing? It has no fixed timeout; React schedules an interruptible background render according to its scheduling priorities.

interview.question: How would you keep a search input responsive?
interview.answer: The input should read the original state, while the expensive child receives the deferred value. That lets the input reflect typing immediately even when rendering the child is slow.
interview.followUp: What visual state can the child expose? It can compare the deferred value with the current value and reduce opacity or otherwise indicate that displayed content is stale.

interview.question: What is initialValue for?
interview.answer: The optional initialValue is used only for the component's initial render. If omitted, the Hook does not defer that first render because React has no earlier value available.
interview.followUp: What happens when the initial value is supplied? React renders with it first and schedules a background render using the deferred value.

keyPoints: Call it at the component's top level and use the returned value for the non-urgent rendering path.
The returned value may temporarily be older than the source value while React prepares the newer result.
React can preserve the previous deferred value for the first update render, keeping the slow path stable.
After urgent work, React attempts the slower render in the background with the latest value.
The source may be a primitive, object, or other value; identity determines whether React sees it as changed.
With initialValue, the first render uses that fallback instead of the supplied value.

Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue init.summary: useDeferredValue(value, initialValue?) returns a deferred version of value. initialValue lets the first render show a baseline value before React updates the deferred view in the background.
Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue init.explanation: Call the Hook at the top level with the value to defer and an optional initial value. When supplied, the initial value is returned for the first render; React then schedules a background re-render using the current value. Later updates can first render with the previous deferred value before updating in the background.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value whose update should be deferred. It can have any type.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: Optional value returned during the component's initial render. If omitted, the initial render is not deferred.

Concurrency hooks::useDeferredValue init.returns: Returns the current deferred value: initialValue on the initial render when supplied, then potentially the previous value during an update before the new value is rendered in the background.

example.title: Use an initial deferred query
example.explanation: The first render uses an empty query, then React schedules a background render using the current query.

useCases.title: Deferred search results
useCases.scenario: A search field should appear immediately while expensive results update later.

useCases.title: Initial loading or baseline view
useCases.scenario: A list or filtered view needs a predictable empty state on its first render.

useCases.title: Responsive secondary UI
useCases.scenario: A non-urgent panel should lag behind urgent controls without blocking them.

interview.question: What does initialValue change in useDeferredValue?
interview.answer: The signature is useDeferredValue(value, initialValue?). On the initial render it returns initialValue when provided; otherwise it returns value. On updates, React can render first with the old value and then render in the background with the new value.
interview.followUp: What happens if initialValue is omitted? The initial render is not deferred because React has no previous value to display.

interview.question: What are the parameters?
interview.answer: value is the value whose updates should be deferred, and it may have any type. initialValue is optional and is used only during the component's initial render.
interview.followUp: Can the Hook defer an object? Yes; the value parameter can have any type, though changing object identity affects when React sees an update.

interview.question: What does the Hook return over time?
interview.answer: The Hook returns the current deferred value. With initialValue, the first result is that initial value; during updates, React may return the previous value first and later return the updated value after a background render.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for loading views? The initial placeholder or filtered state can render immediately while the actual value is rendered afterward in the background.

keyPoints: Use it when a non-critical view should update after more urgent UI, such as an input.
initialValue supplies the first deferred result, which can represent an empty, loading, or baseline view.
When initialValue is supplied, the first render receives it instead of the current value.
After the first render, React schedules work that brings the deferred result up to date.
The deferred input is not limited to strings; objects, arrays, numbers, and other values are allowed.
gotchas: Without initialValue, there is no earlier value to show, so the initial render uses the supplied value immediately.
During updates, the deferred result may temporarily lag behind the source value; code must tolerate that stale value.
Do not call the Hook conditionally, inside loops, or inside nested functions.

Concurrency hooks::useTransition pending.summary: useTransition provides an isPending flag alongside startTransition. Use the flag to show progress or prevent duplicate navigation while a non-blocking transition is underway.
Concurrency hooks::useTransition pending.explanation: Call the Hook at the component’s top level to obtain an isPending boolean and a startTransition function. Put state updates that should be non-blocking inside startTransition; React sets isPending to true when the transition begins and keeps it true until its Actions finish and the final state is displayed.

example.title: Pending tab navigation
example.explanation: The component disables both tab buttons and displays feedback while the transition is pending.

useCases.title: Navigation feedback
useCases.scenario: A tab or route change starts asynchronous rendering; show a pending label while keeping the current UI responsive.

useCases.title: Prevent duplicate navigation
useCases.scenario: A user can click the same navigation control repeatedly before the next screen appears; disable controls while isPending is true.

useCases.title: Non-blocking status
useCases.scenario: A transition updates content without replacing already visible UI; communicate that the new content is still being prepared.

interview.question: What does useTransition return?
interview.answer: useTransition returns exactly two values: isPending and startTransition. isPending reports whether a transition is pending, while startTransition marks synchronous state updates as non-blocking.
interview.followUp: How would you track a transition started outside a component? Use the standalone startTransition, but it does not provide an isPending flag; use useTransition when local pending feedback is required.

interview.question: When is isPending true?
interview.answer: React changes isPending to true when startTransition is first called. It remains true until all Actions complete and the final state is shown to the user.
interview.followUp: What should the UI do with this flag? Use it for feedback such as a pending visual state or to disable controls that would duplicate navigation.

interview.question: How do you use startTransition for navigation?
interview.answer: Pass an action to startTransition and perform the relevant state update inside it. In React 19, the action may be async, allowing pending state to cover asynchronous work.
interview.followUp: What happens after an await? Wrap subsequent state updates in another startTransition so React recognizes them as transition updates.

keyPoints: Destructure the Hook result into isPending for status and startTransition for marking updates.
Use isPending to conditionally render feedback or prevent duplicate user actions.
The Hook must be called at the component’s top level, not conditionally or inside an event handler.
Pending status spans the transition’s Actions through completion of the final visible state.
Show a spinner, pending label, or disabled control while the transition runs.
gotchas: Call useTransition only inside a component or custom Hook; use the standalone startTransition elsewhere.
With async Actions, wrap state updates after each await in another startTransition so those updates remain part of the transition.

Context hooks::use as context.summary: Read a context value with use when the read needs to occur conditionally or inside a loop. Unlike useContext, use supports these positions while still running during render.
Context hooks::use as context.explanation: React's use API reads a context value during rendering. Unlike useContext, it may appear inside conditions and loops, making it suitable when the component should read context only for selected render paths; it still must run inside a component or Hook and cannot be placed in try/catch.

parameters.name: resource
parameters.description: A context object whose current value should be read, or another supported resource such as a Promise.

Context hooks::use as context.returns: Returns the context value when given a context; for a Promise, returns its fulfilled value or suspends/throws according to React's resource handling.

example.title: Conditionally reading context
example.explanation: The component reads the nearest theme only when the divider is rendered, demonstrating conditional context access.

useCases.title: Conditional context access
useCases.scenario: A component returns early or skips a branch unless a feature is enabled, so context is needed only on the active path.

useCases.title: Loop-based reads
useCases.scenario: A component processes several context-bearing resources or values in a repeated render-time operation.

useCases.title: Promise resources
useCases.scenario: A component reads a Promise during rendering and lets React manage its pending, fulfilled, or rejected state.

interview.question: How does use read context, and how does it differ from useContext?
interview.answer: use reads a context value during rendering when passed a context object. It behaves similarly to useContext, but it can be placed in conditional branches and loops.
interview.followUp: Why can use be conditional while useContext cannot? use is designed with special handling that permits these positions, whereas useContext must remain at the component's top level.

interview.question: How do you read a context value with use?
interview.answer: Pass the context object to use, such as use(ThemeContext). React returns the value from the nearest matching provider, or the context's default when no provider supplies one.
interview.followUp: What determines the returned value when providers are nested? The closest provider above the component supplies the value used by the read.

interview.question: What restrictions remain on use despite its conditional-call support?
interview.answer: use may be called in conditions and loops, but the calling function must still be a component or Hook. It is an API used during rendering, not an arbitrary function utility.
interview.followUp: Can use be called inside try/catch? No; the documentation lists try/catch as a restriction even though conditions and loops are allowed.

keyPoints: use reads resources during rendering, including context values and Promises.
Provide a context object as the argument to obtain its current value.
Conditional branches and loops are valid locations for context reads with use.
For context, use follows the same nearest-provider reading model as useContext.
An early return or feature flag can determine whether the component reads context.
gotchas: Do not treat use as unrestricted: although conditional and loop calls are allowed, Promise reads must use the Promise itself each time.
When using use with a Promise, do not inspect its internal status or value directly.

Effect hooks::Hook dependency arrays.summary: Dependency arrays declare every reactive value read by an Effect or memoized calculation. React compares entries with their previous values and re-runs synchronization or calculation when a dependency changes.
Effect hooks::Hook dependency arrays.explanation: A dependency array lists the reactive values read by an Effect or memoized calculation. React compares each entry with its previous value using Object.is; changed entries cause the Effect to re-synchronize or the calculation to run again, while omitted reactive values can leave stale data.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: The setup function that synchronizes with an external system and may return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline, fixed-length list of reactive values referenced by the setup function.

example.title: Declare every reactive value used by an Effect
example.explanation: The Effect reads both serverUrl and roomId, so both appear in its dependency array and trigger re-synchronization when changed.

useCases.title: External-system synchronization
useCases.scenario: Synchronize a chat connection, subscription, timer, or browser widget with current props and state.

useCases.title: Memoized calculations
useCases.scenario: Recompute a cached value when its component inputs change.

useCases.title: Controlled re-synchronization
useCases.scenario: Run an Effect only when its explicitly read reactive inputs change.

interview.question: What belongs in an Effect dependency array?
interview.answer: Include every reactive value read by the Effect: props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component. React uses the list to determine when the Effect must re-synchronize.
interview.followUp: What happens if a reactive value is omitted? The Effect may keep using an outdated value because React does not re-run it when that dependency changes.

interview.question: How does React decide whether dependencies changed?
interview.answer: React compares each dependency with its previous value using Object.is. If any dependency differs, React re-synchronizes the Effect; if none differ, it does not re-run it for that render.
interview.followUp: Why must the array have a constant length? React compares entries by position, so changing the structure makes dependency comparison unreliable.

interview.question: What are the structural rules for a dependency array?
interview.answer: The dependency list must be written inline with a constant number of items, such as [roomId, serverUrl]. An empty array is appropriate only when the Effect reads no reactive values.
interview.followUp: How should a memoized calculation differ? Its array likewise contains every reactive value read by the calculation, and a changed dependency causes React to recompute it.

keyPoints: An Effect’s array must contain every reactive value its code reads; the surrounding code determines the list.
Props, state, and component-scope variables or functions are reactive and generally belong in the array when read.
React checks each entry against its previous render with Object.is to determine whether it changed.
Use [] only when the Effect reads no reactive values.
gotchas: Keep the array inline and fixed-length; do not build it conditionally or change its number of entries between renders.
Do not suppress a dependency merely to control frequency; derive the list from the values the Effect actually reads.

Effect hooks::useEffect.summary: useEffect is a React Hook for synchronizing a component with an external system after rendering. It can return cleanup logic and reruns when its declared dependencies change.
Effect hooks::useEffect.explanation: Call useEffect at the top level with setup code and, optionally, a dependency list. React runs setup after committing the component, reruns it when dependencies change, and invokes the previous cleanup first. Returning cleanup lets the effect undo its external synchronization when dependencies change or the component is removed.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Function containing the effect logic. It may return a cleanup function that reverses the synchronization.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline array of reactive values used by the setup function. It must have a constant length.

example.title: Run an effect when a prop changes
example.explanation: This component updates its displayed status after rendering whenever the online prop changes.

useCases.title: Manage connections
useCases.scenario: Connect to a chat room, websocket, or subscription and disconnect it when the relevant identifier changes or the component unmounts.

useCases.title: Control external widgets
useCases.scenario: Integrate a chart, map, media player, or other imperative widget whose API lives outside React.

useCases.title: Bridge imperative systems
useCases.scenario: Coordinate browser APIs or non-React libraries with current component props and state.

interview.question: When does useEffect run, and what is cleanup for?
interview.answer: useEffect declares synchronization work that React performs after the component commits. Its setup function may return cleanup, which React runs before a changed-dependency setup and when the component is removed.
interview.followUp: What happens when dependencies are omitted? React reruns the effect after every commit, so the effect must tolerate that frequency and clean up correctly.

interview.question: How does React decide whether to rerun an effect?
interview.answer: The second argument is an optional dependency list. React compares each listed dependency with its previous value using Object.is; a changed value causes cleanup with old values followed by setup with new values.
interview.followUp: Why must every reactive value be listed? Otherwise the effect can synchronize using stale props or state, and the linter cannot verify the intended dependency set.

interview.question: What are the calling and return-value rules for useEffect?
interview.answer: useEffect is a Hook and therefore must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook, never inside a loop or condition. It returns undefined, while any cleanup function is returned from the setup function itself.
interview.followUp: When should a visual operation use another effect hook? If work must happen before the browser repaints, consider useLayoutEffect rather than useEffect.

keyPoints: Use it to coordinate React with systems outside React, such as browser APIs, network connections, widgets, or other libraries.
The setup callback runs after the component has been committed, rather than during rendering.
When dependencies change, React stops the previous synchronization before starting the new one.
Dependency changes use Object.is comparisons, so values must remain identical by that comparison to skip rerunning.
Cleanup also runs on unmount, allowing subscriptions, connections, and other external resources to be released.
The Hook itself has no useful return value; return cleanup from setup when teardown is needed.
gotchas: Do not call useEffect inside loops or conditions; move the logic into a component or custom Hook.
Code that must execute during server rendering cannot rely on useEffect.
Do not omit props, state, or other reactive values read by the setup function from the dependency list.
Keep the dependency array inline and do not construct it dynamically or vary its length.

Effect hooks::useEffect cleanup.summary: A useEffect setup function may return cleanup logic. React runs cleanup before an Effect re-runs with changed dependencies and when the component is removed, allowing external work to be undone or stale asynchronous results to be ignored.
Effect hooks::useEffect cleanup.explanation: A cleanup function is the optional function returned by an Effect's setup. React runs it before re-running the Effect when dependencies change and when the component is removed, so it can undo the previous setup, disconnect external resources, remove listeners, or prevent stale asynchronous work from being used.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Function containing the Effect logic; it may return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline array with a constant number of dependencies. React compares each with its previous value using Object.is.

Effect hooks::useEffect cleanup.returns: The page documents the setup callback's optional cleanup function; React invokes it before setup after dependency changes and when the component is removed from the DOM.

example.title: Ignore stale fetch results
example.explanation: The cleanup marks an earlier request obsolete so a late response cannot update results for a newer query.

useCases.title: Disconnect external services
useCases.scenario: An Effect opens a connection or subscription; cleanup closes or unsubscribes it before replacement or removal.

useCases.title: Remove event listeners
useCases.scenario: An Effect registers a browser or third-party listener; cleanup removes the corresponding listener.

useCases.title: Handle asynchronous work
useCases.scenario: An Effect starts a request whose result may become obsolete; cleanup aborts it or ignores its result.

interview.question: When does a useEffect cleanup function run?
interview.answer: React runs cleanup after a commit when dependencies changed, before setup runs with the new values. It also runs cleanup when the component is removed from the DOM.
interview.followUp: Why can cleanup run without unmounting? Because changed dependencies require the old Effect instance to be stopped before the new one starts.

interview.question: How do you define Effect cleanup?
interview.answer: Return a function from the setup callback. That function should disconnect, unsubscribe, remove listeners, abort work, or otherwise undo the setup; if no cleanup is needed, return nothing.
interview.followUp: How should fetch work be handled? Cleanup can abort the fetch or ignore its result so stale data does not win a race.

interview.question: How do dependencies control cleanup timing?
interview.answer: React compares the dependency list with its previous value using Object.is. If a dependency changed, React performs cleanup with the old values and then runs setup with the new values.
interview.followUp: What happens when the dependency argument is omitted? The Effect runs after every commit, so its cleanup can also run before every subsequent setup.

keyPoints: The setup callback can return a function that performs cleanup.
Dependency changes cause cleanup to run before the next setup.
Cleanup observes the previous Effect inputs, while the replacement setup receives the new ones.
Unmounting invokes the final cleanup for the component.
Keep the dependency array inline and fixed in length.
React uses Object.is semantics to decide whether an Effect needs replacement.
For asynchronous fetching, cleanup must cancel the request or suppress stale results.
gotchas: Cleanup is not limited to unmounting; dependency changes trigger it before the next setup.
Development Strict Mode performs an extra setup-cleanup cycle, so cleanup must tolerate this stress test.
Cleanup should reverse or stop the work established by setup rather than perform unrelated actions.

Effect hooks::useEffectEvent.summary: useEffectEvent creates a non-reactive Effect Event that can read the latest props and state without making the calling Effect re-synchronize. Call it only from Effects, and keep it out of dependency arrays.
Effect hooks::useEffectEvent.explanation: useEffectEvent extracts non-reactive logic from an Effect into a function that still reads the latest committed props and state when called. Declare it at component or custom-Hook top level, invoke it only from an Effect or another Effect Event, and omit it from Effect dependencies.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: A callback containing the Effect Event logic; it may accept any number of arguments and return any value.

Effect hooks::useEffectEvent.returns: An Effect Event function with the same type signature as the callback. It accesses the latest committed render values when called.

example.title: Use current theme without reconnecting
example.explanation: The connection reacts to roomId, while onConnected reads the latest theme without causing reconnection.

useCases.title: Separate connection lifecycle from notification behavior
useCases.scenario: A subscription must stay connected to the same resource while its notification uses the latest theme or preference.

useCases.title: Read current state from a stable subscription
useCases.scenario: A message listener needs current state such as mute preferences without recreating the subscription whenever that state changes.

useCases.title: Extract non-reactive Effect logic
useCases.scenario: An Effect performs an event-like action whose inputs should be fresh at invocation time but should not determine synchronization.

interview.question: What problem does useEffectEvent solve?
interview.answer: useEffectEvent creates a function whose callback sees the latest committed props and state when invoked. Unlike ordinary Effect logic, that callback is non-reactive, so values it reads do not cause the surrounding Effect to re-synchronize.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent a chat connection from restarting when the theme changes? Extract the notification into useEffectEvent, call it from the connection Effect, and keep roomId—not theme—in the Effect dependencies.

interview.question: What does useEffectEvent accept and return?
interview.answer: The callback argument contains the Effect Event logic and may accept any number of arguments and return any value. The Hook returns an Effect Event with the callback's same type signature.
interview.followUp: Where may the returned function run? Inside useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useInsertionEffect, or another Effect Event in the same component.

interview.question: Should an Effect Event be included in an Effect dependency array?
interview.answer: Effect Events are intended for event-like work that an Effect triggers, not for every function inside an Effect. They should not be added to the dependency array because they always read current committed values without making the Effect reactive to those values.
interview.followUp: What should happen if logic is genuinely reactive? Keep it in the Effect and declare every reactive value it reads as a dependency instead of hiding it in an Effect Event.

keyPoints: Use the Hook to move event-like, non-reactive work out of an Effect while keeping it associated with that Effect.
Create the Effect Event at the component's top level or inside a custom Hook.
The callback reads current committed props and state when called, without making the surrounding Effect restart.
Invoke the returned function from any supported Effect Hook or from another Effect Event in the same component.
Treat an Effect Event as Effect-owned event logic: it is triggered by an Effect rather than directly by a user interaction.
gotchas: Call the returned function only from an Effect or another Effect Event; do not invoke it during rendering.
Do not call an Effect Event during render or pass it to another component or Hook.
Because it is a Hook, declare useEffectEvent at the top level rather than inside a loop or condition.

Effect hooks::useEffectEvent limitations.summary: useEffectEvent extracts non-reactive logic from an Effect. It can read the latest props and state without resynchronizing the Effect, but it must be called only from Effects and is not a general-purpose event handler replacement.
Effect hooks::useEffectEvent limitations.explanation: useEffectEvent extracts non-reactive logic that an Effect triggers. Its callback can read current props and state without being an Effect dependency, but the function is restricted to Effect execution and should remain next to the Effect that uses it.
Effect hooks::useEffectEvent limitations.returns: A function representing the Effect Event.

example.title: Use an Effect Event from an Effect
example.explanation: The Effect Event reads the latest theme without making the connection Effect resynchronize when only theme changes.

useCases.title: Read fresh values in an external subscription
useCases.scenario: An Effect subscribes to an external system and needs current props or state inside a callback without reconnecting when those values change.

useCases.title: Separate non-reactive Effect logic
useCases.scenario: An Effect triggers a conceptual event whose logic should not independently make the Effect reactive.

interview.question: What is an Effect Event, and how does it differ from a normal event handler?
interview.answer: An Effect Event is a non-reactive callback extracted from an Effect. It reads the latest props and state, but it is triggered only by an Effect or another Effect Event, not by rendering or ordinary user interaction.
interview.followUp: How should a callback used by a button be handled? Use a normal event handler; Effect Events are for events fired by Effects.

interview.question: Where may an Effect Event be called?
interview.answer: Call the function only inside useEffect, useLayoutEffect, useInsertionEffect, or another Effect Event. Do not call it during render or pass it to another component or Hook.
interview.followUp: What catches these violations? The eslint-plugin-react-hooks linter enforces the restriction.

interview.question: When should useEffectEvent not be used?
interview.answer: Use it only when part of an Effect is genuinely event-like and should read current values without causing the surrounding Effect to resynchronize. It must not be used merely to remove values from the dependency array.
interview.followUp: Why is dependency suppression dangerous? It can conceal synchronization bugs and make the code harder to understand.

keyPoints: An Effect Event observes current props and state while leaving the surrounding Effect’s synchronization behavior unchanged.
Its valid callers include all three built-in Effect hooks and another Effect Event in the same component.
Declare useEffectEvent at Hook top level, never inside a condition or loop.
The Hook is intended for Effect-triggered event logic, not as a general-purpose callback wrapper.
Treat the returned function as identity-unstable because it changes across renders.
gotchas: Do not use useEffectEvent as a way to suppress legitimate dependencies; doing so can hide bugs and make the Effect harder to understand.
Calling one during render, from a user event handler, or from arbitrary code violates its intended usage.
Keep the Effect Event local to the component or Hook containing the Effect that triggers it.
Do not depend on an Effect Event function having stable identity.

Effect hooks::useInsertionEffect.summary: A specialized effect for CSS-in-JS libraries to insert styles before layout effects run. It runs on the client and returns undefined; ordinary application code generally should not need it.
Effect hooks::useInsertionEffect.explanation: Call this Hook from a CSS-in-JS library to synchronously install styles at the insertion phase. React runs setup when the component enters the DOM, runs cleanup before setup when dependencies change, and runs cleanup on removal. It returns undefined; it is client-only, refs are not attached yet, state updates are forbidden, and DOM-update timing is not guaranteed.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Effect setup logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline list of all reactive values referenced by setup.

example.title: Insert a generated style rule
example.explanation: A CSS-in-JS-style hook inserts a style element before layout effects and removes the old element when the rule changes or the component unmounts.

useCases.title: Inject dynamic CSS
useCases.scenario: A CSS-in-JS library creates or updates a style element when a generated rule changes.

useCases.title: Prepare styles before layout effects
useCases.scenario: A library must make styles available before another effect measures layout.

useCases.title: Manage style lifecycles
useCases.scenario: A library replaces an old generated rule and needs deterministic cleanup.

interview.question: What is useInsertionEffect for?
interview.answer: useInsertionEffect is intended for CSS-in-JS library authors. It lets a library insert styles before layout effects run, so layout-reading effects can observe the intended styling.
interview.followUp: Why should ordinary application code usually avoid it? Because it has unusual timing constraints: refs are unavailable, state updates are disallowed, and DOM-update timing is not fixed.

interview.question: How do setup, cleanup, and dependencies work?
interview.answer: Its signature is useInsertionEffect(setup, dependencies?). The setup function may return cleanup; React runs setup on insertion, cleanup then setup after changed dependencies, and cleanup on unmount.
interview.followUp: What must dependencies contain? Every reactive value referenced by setup, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component.

interview.question: What are its main constraints?
interview.answer: The Hook returns undefined and runs only on the client. Its execution is not a reliable point for reading an updated DOM because it may run before or after DOM mutation.
interview.followUp: Can it update state or use refs? No: state updates are prohibited and refs have not been attached when it runs.

keyPoints: Use it primarily inside a CSS-in-JS library, not for routine component effects.
Its insertion phase precedes layout effects, allowing style elements to be installed before layout measurement.
Return cleanup to remove or replace inserted resources.
When dependencies change, React cleans up the previous installation before applying the new one.
Dependencies cover props, state, and component-local variables or functions used by setup.
gotchas: Do not update state from this Hook; use another effect or an event instead.
Do not read refs here because React has not attached them at this phase.
Never depend on the DOM already having been updated when this Hook runs.
The insertion effect does not execute during server rendering.

Effect hooks::useLayoutEffect.summary: Use useLayoutEffect for layout measurement or visual corrections that must happen before the browser paints. Prefer useEffect unless pre-paint timing is necessary.
Effect hooks::useLayoutEffect.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs after React commits DOM changes but before the browser repaints. Use it when an effect must read layout or synchronously adjust visual state without exposing an intermediate position; otherwise prefer useEffect because layout effects and their state updates block repaint.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Function containing the effect logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline list of reactive values referenced by setup; omit it to run after every commit.

example.title: Measure an element before paint
example.explanation: Measures the rendered tooltip before repaint and stores its height for layout-dependent rendering.

useCases.title: Measure and position an overlay
useCases.scenario: A tooltip or popover must be positioned from its measured dimensions before the first visible paint.

useCases.title: Synchronize layout-dependent state
useCases.scenario: A component needs to read an element's bounding rectangle and update state before the user sees an intermediate layout.

useCases.title: Perform client-only layout work
useCases.scenario: A client-side component integrates a DOM measurement or visual adjustment that cannot run during server rendering.

interview.question: When should useLayoutEffect be preferred over useEffect?
interview.answer: useLayoutEffect is a pre-paint variant of useEffect. It is useful for measuring DOM layout or applying visual corrections before the user sees the result.
interview.followUp: What is the cost? Its code and state updates block repaint, so ordinary effects should remain useEffect.

interview.question: What are the arguments to useLayoutEffect?
interview.answer: The setup function contains the effect logic and may return cleanup logic. The optional dependency list contains reactive values used by setup and controls when React re-synchronizes the effect.
interview.followUp: What must be true of the dependency list? It should contain every reactive value referenced by setup and have a constant number of items written inline.

interview.question: What does useLayoutEffect return, and where can it run?
interview.answer: It runs only on the client, not during server rendering, and returns undefined. It must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook.
interview.followUp: How can server-rendered code avoid depending on it? Render a server-safe initial result and perform client-only measurement after hydration.

keyPoints: It is designed for effects whose timing must precede the next browser paint.
A typical use is reading an element's geometry before displaying a layout-dependent result.
Return cleanup code when the effect creates subscriptions, listeners, or other resources that need removal.
The dependency list should include every reactive value read by the setup function.
This Hook does not provide a value to the component.
gotchas: Call it only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; never inside loops or conditions.
Server-rendered components cannot rely on this Hook for server-side work.
Keep the work small because excessive use can slow the application.

External store hooks::useDebugValue.summary: useDebugValue adds a readable label or debug value for a custom Hook in React DevTools. It is for inspection only: it does not change the Hook's runtime behavior or return a value.
External store hooks::useDebugValue.explanation: Call useDebugValue inside a custom Hook to expose a readable value in React DevTools. React uses the first argument directly unless you provide a second formatting function; that formatter receives the value when the component is inspected and returns what DevTools displays. The Hook itself has no return value and does not alter the custom Hook's runtime result.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to expose in React DevTools; it may have any type.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Optional formatter called with value during component inspection; its returned value is displayed.

example.title: Label a custom Hook
example.explanation: Adds an Online or Offline label for this custom Hook when its consumer is inspected in React DevTools.

useCases.title: Show a readable status
useCases.scenario: A custom Hook exposes a boolean or status enum

useCases.title: Format complex inspection data
useCases.scenario: A custom Hook exposes structured state

useCases.title: Make library Hooks easier to inspect
useCases.scenario: A library publishes custom Hooks for application teams

interview.question: What problem does useDebugValue solve?
interview.answer: useDebugValue adds a label or debug value for a custom Hook in React DevTools. It is intended for inspecting components that use the custom Hook and does not provide a runtime value to the component.
interview.followUp: How can the displayed value be customized? Pass a second argument, a formatter that receives the debug value and returns the value DevTools should display.

interview.question: What are the arguments to useDebugValue?
interview.answer: Its signature is useDebugValue(value, format?). The value can be any type; the optional format function receives that value when the component is inspected and returns the formatted display value.
interview.followUp: What happens when format is omitted? React DevTools displays the original value directly.

interview.question: What does useDebugValue return, and how does it affect a custom Hook's API?
interview.answer: useDebugValue returns nothing. A custom Hook can call it to expose inspection information while continuing to return its own state, data, or API to consumers.
interview.followUp: Where should it be called? At the top level of the custom Hook, following the Rules of Hooks.

keyPoints: It exposes a developer-facing label for a custom Hook in React DevTools.
Place the call directly at the custom Hook's top level to make its inspection value available.
The first argument is the debug value that DevTools should show.
The debug value is not restricted to strings; it may use any JavaScript type.
The optional second argument transforms the debug value into a display value.
A formatter accepts the supplied value and returns the representation intended for inspection.
Treat the Hook as an inspection side effect; it does not produce a value for your custom Hook to return.
gotchas: The formatter is invoked during inspection, so avoid unnecessary expensive formatting work in the custom Hook.
Keep the call at the custom Hook's top level rather than placing it inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
Without a formatter, DevTools shows the raw debug value, which may be less readable than an intentional display value.

External store hooks::useDebugValue form.summary: useDebugValue lets a custom Hook expose a readable label in React DevTools. An optional formatter transforms the label only when DevTools inspects the component, avoiding unnecessary formatting work during ordinary use.
External store hooks::useDebugValue form.explanation: Call useDebugValue at the top level of a custom Hook with its internal value and an optional formatter. React DevTools invokes that formatter when the component is inspected, then displays the returned value; without a formatter, it displays the original value. The Hook itself has no return value.

parameters.description: The value to display in React DevTools; it may have any type.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Optional function that receives value and returns the formatted display value used by React DevTools.

useCases.title: Readable status diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Expose a readable online/offline state instead of an internal boolean.

useCases.title: Lazy expensive formatting
useCases.scenario: Convert dates or other complex values into concise DevTools labels only when inspected.

useCases.title: Custom Hook inspection
useCases.scenario: Make reusable custom Hooks easier to understand while debugging consuming components.

interview.question: What problem does useDebugValue solve?
interview.answer: useDebugValue adds a label for a custom Hook in React DevTools. Its first argument is the value shown by default, and an optional second argument transforms that value for display when the component is inspected.
interview.followUp: What happens when the formatter is omitted? React DevTools displays the original value itself.

interview.question: How does the formatter argument work?
interview.answer: The formatter receives the debug value as its argument and returns the value React DevTools should display. The returned value can be any type.
interview.followUp: When does the formatter run? It runs when DevTools inspects the component, not as part of every normal render.

interview.question: Where should useDebugValue be called, and what does it return?
interview.answer: useDebugValue does not return anything. It is called at the top level of the custom Hook to expose a readable diagnostic value to React DevTools.
interview.followUp: Why use a formatter for expensive formatting? Delaying the transformation until inspection avoids doing that work when the component is not being inspected.

keyPoints: Use it to expose a custom Hook's diagnostic label in React DevTools.
Invoke it at the custom Hook's top level to publish a readable diagnostic value.
The value argument is the underlying diagnostic data to expose.
The debug value is not restricted to a particular JavaScript type.
Omitting format makes DevTools display the untransformed value.
A formatter accepts the debug value and returns the representation intended for DevTools.
gotchas: The formatter is not called during ordinary rendering; DevTools calls it when the component is inspected.
Place the call at the custom Hook's top level rather than inside conditions or nested functions.

External store hooks::useSyncExternalSto.summary: Subscribe to an external store or changing browser value without manually coordinating an Effect. React reads a stable snapshot, responds to store notifications, and cleans up the subscription when needed.
External store hooks::useSyncExternalSto.explanation: Call this Hook at the top level with a stable subscription function and a snapshot reader. React invokes the callback when the browser source changes, rechecks the snapshot, compares it with Object.is, and re-renders when the snapshot differs; the returned cleanup function removes the event listeners.

parameters.name: subscribe
parameters.description: Function receiving one callback, registering it with the external store, and returning cleanup that removes the subscription.

parameters.name: getSnapshot
parameters.description: Function returning the component's needed store snapshot. It must return the same value while the store is unchanged.

parameters.name: getServerSnapshot
parameters.description: Optional function returning the snapshot used during server rendering and client hydration.
