useCases.title: Connect to an external state store
useCases.scenario: A component reads data from a state library or other store that is managed outside React.

useCases.title: Supply server and hydration snapshots
useCases.scenario: The application renders on the server and must provide a browser-independent initial value during hydration.

interview.question: What do subscribe and getSnapshot do?
interview.answer: useSyncExternalStore connects a component to data managed outside React. The subscribe function registers a callback and returns cleanup, while getSnapshot reads the current value; React rechecks that value after notifications and renders if Object.is detects a change.
interview.followUp: Why must getSnapshot be stable when the store is unchanged? React may call it repeatedly during rendering, so an unstable result could trigger unnecessary renders or violate concurrent-rendering consistency.

interview.question: How do you subscribe to a browser value such as online status?
interview.answer: For browser APIs, getSnapshot reads the current browser value and subscribe listens for the events that can change it. For online status, navigator.onLine is the snapshot and window online/offline events notify React.
interview.followUp: How would server rendering change the implementation? Add getServerSnapshot as the third argument and return a server-safe value, because browser APIs are unavailable during server rendering.

interview.question: How does React receive updated external-store data?
interview.answer: The Hook must be called at the top level of the component. The subscription callback tells React that the source may have changed; React then calls getSnapshot again rather than receiving the new value directly from the callback.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the component unmounts? React calls the cleanup function returned by subscribe, which should unregister every listener installed by the subscription.

keyPoints: Use the Hook when the data source lives outside React state, including a mutable browser API.
Invoke it unconditionally at component top level rather than inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
Make subscribe install the source listener and return matching cleanup so unmounted components stop receiving notifications.
The callback is a notification signal: React obtains the current value by calling getSnapshot again.
A re-render depends on the snapshot changing according to Object.is, not merely on a notification being emitted.
A suitable browser source provides both a current value and events that announce changes.
gotchas: Ensure the snapshot is cached or otherwise stable until the external source actually changes; returning a newly created value on every call is invalid.

External store hooks::useSyncExternalSto.summary: Provide getServerSnapshot as the third argument to useSyncExternalStore when rendering an external store on the server. It must yield the same initial snapshot on the server and during client hydration.
External store hooks::useSyncExternalSto.explanation: Pass getServerSnapshot as the third argument when an external-store component can render on the server. React uses it to produce the server HTML and to initialize the client during hydration, so it must return the same initial data on both sides; the value is commonly serialized from server to client.

parameters.name: subscribe
parameters.description: Function that subscribes React to the external store and returns an unsubscribe function.

parameters.name: getSnapshot
parameters.description: Function that reads and returns the store's current snapshot.

parameters.name: getServerSnapshot
parameters.description: Optional function returning the initial store snapshot for server rendering and client hydration.

External store hooks::useSyncExternalSto.returns: Returns the current snapshot from the external store.

example.title: Provide a hydration-safe server snapshot
example.explanation: The third argument supplies the value used for server rendering and client hydration; here, both initially use the same online state.

useCases.title: Server rendering
useCases.scenario: An external store is read by a component rendered into server-generated HTML.

useCases.title: Consistent hydration
useCases.scenario: A client takes over markup produced by the server.

useCases.title: Serialized store bootstrap
useCases.scenario: The initial store value must cross the server-client boundary without divergence.

interview.question: What is getServerSnapshot used for?
interview.answer: getServerSnapshot is the optional third argument to useSyncExternalStore. It returns the store's initial value for server rendering and for the client's hydration pass.
interview.followUp: What must happen when the store changes before hydration? The initial client snapshot still needs to match the server output; subsequent store updates can then be reflected normally.

interview.question: When does getServerSnapshot run?
interview.answer: It runs in two contexts: while the server generates HTML and while the client hydrates that HTML. It is not the normal ongoing client subscription reader.
interview.followUp: Why is serialization useful? It lets the client reconstruct the same server snapshot instead of independently producing a potentially different value.

interview.question: How do you prevent hydration mismatches?
interview.answer: The server and client must receive the same exact initial snapshot. In practice, the server commonly serializes the store data and passes it to the client.
interview.followUp: What is the consequence of omitting the third argument for an SSR component? Server rendering throws an error.

keyPoints: getServerSnapshot supplies the store's initial snapshot for server-aware rendering.
React limits this callback to HTML generation on the server and the corresponding client hydration phase.
The initial store data must agree across environments so hydrated markup starts from the same state.
A common implementation transfers the server's initial store data to the browser through serialization.
Use getSnapshot for ordinary store reads and reserve this callback for the two server-related phases.
During server rendering, React calls it to determine the external-store value represented in generated HTML.
During hydration, React calls it before the component switches to normal client-side store behavior.
gotchas: A server-rendered component must provide getServerSnapshot; leaving it out causes server rendering to fail.
Do not compute different initial values on the two environments, or hydration can become inconsistent.
The client's first render must reproduce the server's exact snapshot, not merely an equivalent-looking value.

Hook patterns::Callback refs.summary: A callback ref is a function passed to ref that receives a node on attachment and can return cleanup logic for detachment. It ties setup and teardown directly to the node lifecycle, avoiding an Effect for this pattern.
Hook patterns::Callback refs.explanation: A callback ref is a function passed to the ref prop. React invokes it with the DOM node when the node attaches; the function may return cleanup logic that React invokes when the node detaches. Keep the callback stable when possible, because changing the callback causes React to detach the old ref and attach the new one.
Hook patterns::Callback refs.syntax: const refCallback = (node: T | null) => { /* setup */ return () => { /* cleanup */ }; };

parameters.name: node
parameters.description: The DOM node or component instance supplied by React when the ref attaches; compatibility detachment may supply null.

Hook patterns::Callback refs.returns: Optional cleanup function invoked when the ref is detached; without one, React uses the compatibility null-callback behavior.

example.title: Attach and detach with a callback ref
example.explanation: The callback runs with the input node when it attaches and returns cleanup logic for detachment.

useCases.title: Per-node DOM setup
useCases.scenario: A node must be focused or measured immediately when React attaches it.

useCases.title: Managing collections of refs
useCases.scenario: A list needs a Map or array of currently mounted nodes keyed by ID or index.

useCases.title: Paired attachment and cleanup
useCases.scenario: Node-specific listeners or registrations must be removed exactly when the node detaches.

interview.question: When does React invoke a callback ref?
interview.answer: React calls a callback ref with the DOM node when the node is attached. If the callback returns a cleanup function, React calls that function when the node is detached.
interview.followUp: What happens if the callback ref identity changes? React cleans up or detaches the previous callback, then invokes the new callback with the node.

interview.question: Why use a callback ref instead of an Effect for node setup?
interview.answer: A callback ref can perform node-specific setup immediately when React provides the node, such as focusing it or registering it in a collection. Its returned function performs the matching teardown when React removes the node.
interview.followUp: Why can this be preferable to an Effect for node attachment? The lifecycle is directly tied to that particular node's ref attachment and detachment.

interview.question: What changed for callback refs in React 19?
interview.answer: React 19 added cleanup functions for ref callbacks. Returning cleanup avoids relying on the compatibility behavior where React calls the callback with null during detachment.
interview.followUp: What does Strict Mode test? It runs an extra development setup-cleanup cycle, exposing setup that is not properly reversed.

keyPoints: Pass a function to the ref prop to create a callback ref rather than using a ref object.
The callback receives the attached DOM node, allowing setup that needs the actual node.
Return a cleanup function to run node-specific teardown when React clears the ref.
Changing the callback function causes React to process the old ref and the new ref, even if the DOM node remains.
React 19 introduced the returned-cleanup form for callback refs.
gotchas: An inline callback ref changes identity on every render, so React detaches the previous ref and attaches the new one. Define it outside JSX or memoize it when repeated setup is undesirable.
Strict Mode intentionally performs an additional development setup and cleanup cycle; cleanup must fully undo setup.
For compatibility, omitting a cleanup function makes React call the callback with null on detachment; returning cleanup is the modern React 19 pattern.

Hook patterns::Custom Hook naming.summary: Custom Hook names must start with `use` followed by a capital letter. Use this prefix when the function calls at least one Hook; otherwise, keep it as a regular function.
Hook patterns::Custom Hook naming.explanation: A custom Hook is a JavaScript function whose name begins with `use` followed by a capital letter when it calls one or more Hooks. This naming convention lets React’s tooling recognize it as a Hook and lets it follow Hook-call rules. Functions that call no Hooks should remain ordinary functions without the `use` prefix.
Hook patterns::Custom Hook naming.syntax: function useHookName(/* parameters */) { /* Hook calls and reusable logic */ }

example.title: A correctly named custom Hook
example.explanation: The custom Hook starts with `use`, calls a Hook internally, and returns a value for the component to render.

useCases.title: Compose Hooks

useCases.title: Avoid a misleading Hook name
useCases.scenario: Keep a rendering helper that calls no Hooks as an ordinary function.

keyPoints: Name a custom Hook with `use` and then an uppercase letter, such as `useOnlineStatus`.
A function that calls at least one Hook should use the `use` prefix, making it a custom Hook.
A custom Hook is not restricted to returning state; it can return any value useful to its caller.
Use custom Hooks to package reusable stateful logic for multiple components.
gotchas: Do not add `use` to a function merely because it is called during rendering; reserve the prefix for functions that call Hooks.

Hook patterns::Deriving instead of stori.summary: Derive values from props and existing state during render instead of storing redundant copies. This keeps one source of truth and avoids synchronization bugs.
Hook patterns::Deriving instead of stori.explanation: Keep state to the minimal changing information the component must remember. If a value can be calculated from current props or existing state during render, derive it there instead of creating another state variable; use a memoization Hook only when recomputation is actually a concern.

keyPoints: Compute values from current props and state during render instead of storing copies in state.
A derivable value is redundant state and creates another value that must remain synchronized.
For example, concatenate two stored name fields when rendering rather than storing fullName separately.
Removing duplicate state reduces synchronization work and prevents stale derived values.
Read a prop directly when the component should reflect its latest value.
gotchas: Mirroring a prop into state makes the state stop following later prop changes. Use the prop directly unless intentionally keeping an initial or otherwise fixed snapshot.

Hook patterns::Effect race conditions.summary: Prevent stale asynchronous responses from updating state after an Effect is no longer current. Capture an `ignore` flag and set it during cleanup before checking it when the response arrives.
Hook patterns::Effect race conditions.explanation: An Effect that starts a request can receive responses out of order. Keep an ignore flag inside the Effect, check it before applying the response, and set it during cleanup so only the still-active Effect updates state.

parameters.name: dependencies

example.explanation: Each Effect run owns its local flag. Cleanup marks that run inactive, so a later response cannot overwrite state for the current person.

Requests can finish out of order; guarding the state update prevents an older response from winning.
Fetching data is a valid Effect use case when the request synchronizes the component with an external system.

Hook patterns::eslint-plugin-react-hooks.summary: `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` provides ESLint rules that enforce React’s hook constraints. Use `rules-of-hooks` for stable call order and `exhaustive-deps` for complete dependency arrays, catching common bugs before runtime.
Hook patterns::eslint-plugin-react-hooks.explanation: The plugin supplies ESLint rules for React’s hook constraints and dependency arrays. `rules-of-hooks` checks that hooks execute in a consistent order, while `exhaustive-deps` checks that values referenced by hooks appear in their dependency arrays, helping catch state mismatches and stale closures during development.
Hook patterns::eslint-plugin-react-hooks.syntax: eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended preset: rules-of-hooks and exhaustive-deps

example.explanation: The component calls hooks unconditionally at the top level, while the effect lists the reactive value it reads. The plugin can flag conditional hook calls and incomplete dependency arrays.

useCases.scenario: A component conditionally calls `useState`, `useEffect`, or another hook.

useCases.title: Detect incomplete dependencies
useCases.scenario: An effect, memo, or callback reads changing values.

useCases.title: Extend dependency linting
useCases.scenario: A codebase defines custom effect hooks.

useCases.title: Validate broader React patterns

interview.question: What problem does `rules-of-hooks` prevent?
interview.answer: `rules-of-hooks` verifies that components and hooks follow the Rules of Hooks. React depends on the exact same hooks being called in the exact same order on every render, so the rule catches conditional, looped, or otherwise misplaced hook calls.
interview.followUp: How can custom effect hooks be linted? Configure the shared `react-hooks.additionalEffectHooks` setting with a regular expression matching their names; this configuration is used by both relevant lint rules.

interview.question: What does `exhaustive-deps` detect?
interview.answer: `exhaustive-deps` checks dependency arrays for hooks such as `useEffect`, `useMemo`, and `useCallback`. Missing a referenced dependency can prevent reruns or recalculation when that value changes, producing a stale closure.
interview.followUp: What happens if both shared and rule-level custom-hook configuration is present? The rule-level `additionalHooks` option takes precedence for that rule.

interview.question: What else does the recommended preset cover?
interview.answer: The plugin is broader than the two foundational hook rules: its recommended preset also includes checks related to purity, refs, immutability, state updates, component factories, and React Compiler configuration. This lets ESLint catch additional violations at build time.
interview.followUp: Why should components and hooks generally be defined at module scope? Nested definitions create new instances on calls or renders, which can destroy state and cause performance problems.

keyPoints: Install and enable the plugin when you want ESLint to enforce React-specific correctness constraints rather than relying only on code review.
The `rules-of-hooks` rule protects hook order, so state remains associated with the intended hook across renders.
Call hooks at the top level of components or custom hooks; do not make their execution conditional.
The recommended preset includes both `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` among its checks.
gotchas: Do not place hooks in conditions or loops: changing whether a hook runs changes the call order React uses to preserve state.

Hook patterns::Hooks and StrictMode.summary: StrictMode adds development-only checks for a component subtree. It repeats rendering and runs an extra Effect setup-cleanup cycle to expose impure renders and missing cleanup.
Hook patterns::Hooks and StrictMode.explanation: StrictMode adds development-only checks around a component tree. It invokes rendering again to expose impure render logic and performs an additional Effect setup-and-cleanup cycle to reveal missing cleanup, while preserving state and DOM during the simulated remount.
Hook patterns::Hooks and StrictMode.returns: A React element that enables additional development checks for its descendants.

example.explanation: The cleanup makes the Effect safe when development StrictMode performs an extra setup-and-cleanup cycle.

useCases.scenario: Enable development diagnostics around an application or feature subtree.

useCases.title: Test Effect cleanup
useCases.scenario: Verify subscriptions, connections, timers, and other Effect-managed resources are released.

useCases.title: Test ref cleanup
useCases.scenario: Check callback refs that acquire resources or mutate external systems.

interview.question: What does StrictMode do to Hooks-related behavior?
interview.answer: StrictMode is a development-only wrapper that enables extra checks for the enclosed component tree. It re-renders components to detect impure rendering and re-runs Effects to expose missing cleanup.
interview.followUp: What should an Effect guarantee? Its setup should be safely repeatable, and its cleanup should fully reverse the setup so an additional setup-cleanup cycle leaves no unwanted external state.

interview.question: Why might an Effect appear to run twice?
interview.answer: On initial development mounting, React performs an extra Effect setup-and-cleanup cycle. This simulates the kind of lifecycle sequence that can reveal subscriptions, connections, or other resources that were not cleaned up.
interview.followUp: Why is this not treated as a production double mount? The behavior is development-only and is intended as a stress test rather than an application runtime contract.

interview.question: What does StrictMode reveal about component purity?
interview.answer: StrictMode also calls component functions an extra time during development to find impure rendering. Rendering should therefore be free of mutations or other side effects that depend on being called only once.
interview.followUp: Where should an interaction-driven side effect go? Prefer an event handler; use an Effect for synchronization with an external system when the behavior is caused by rendering.

keyPoints: Wrap a component subtree in StrictMode to detect lifecycle and purity problems before production.
Component rendering must be pure because development StrictMode may invoke it again.
Effect cleanup is tested by an additional development run.
Ref callbacks also need cleanup when they acquire or register external resources.
An Effect’s setup and cleanup should tolerate repetition without accumulating subscriptions or resources.
gotchas: An Effect must undo or stop whatever its setup starts; otherwise the extra development cycle can expose leaks or duplicated subscriptions.
A nested StrictMode boundary does not perform the initial extra Effect cycle when that behavior would create an impossible production sequence.

Keep Hook calls static, pure, and inside React components or custom Hooks; when the compiler detects a violation, it skips optimizing the affected component or Hook rather than changing its behavior.

Its automatic memoization is intended to reduce unnecessary updates in compiled React code.

Manual memoization remains available when precise control over a particular value or callback is needed.

Hook patterns::useContext default values.summary: useContext returns the closest matching provider value. If no matching provider exists above the consumer, it returns the static defaultValue supplied to createContext; an explicit undefined provider value is not replaced by that default.
Hook patterns::useContext default values.explanation: Pass a fallback to createContext when defining the context. useContext returns that fallback only when no matching provider exists above the consumer; a provider whose value is undefined still supplies undefined. Because the fallback is static, use state and a provider value when the context must change. A null fallback can be checked and turned into a clear error when the provider is required.

useCases.scenario: A required provider should be detected close to the consuming component.

Treat the fallback as a fixed baseline, not reactive context state.
A context may use null when there is no meaningful standalone fallback.

The relevant provider must be above the component reading the context.

Performance hooks::useCallback.summary: useCallback caches a function definition between renders. React reuses its identity while the listed dependencies remain unchanged, which can help memoized children or Hooks that depend on the callback.
Performance hooks::useCallback.explanation: Call useCallback at the top level with a function and every reactive value that function reads. React returns the initial function first; later it returns the cached function when dependencies remain Object.is-equal, otherwise it returns the current function.

parameters.name: fn

parameters.name: dependencies

example.title: Stabilize a callback passed to a memoized child
example.explanation: The callback keeps the same identity while draft is unchanged, allowing the memoized button to skip renders caused by unrelated parent updates.

useCases.title: Memoized child props
useCases.scenario: A callback is passed as a prop to a child optimized with memo, and a stable prop identity can avoid unnecessary child renders.

useCases.title: Hook dependencies
useCases.scenario: A callback is referenced by an Effect or another Hook dependency list, and its identity should change only when its captured values change.

useCases.title: Custom Hook API
useCases.scenario: A component needs to expose a stable callback from a custom Hook for consumers that compare function references.

interview.question: What does useCallback return when dependencies do not change?
interview.answer: useCallback caches a function definition between renders. It returns the prior function when every dependency compares equal with Object.is, and otherwise returns the function supplied for the current render.
interview.followUp: Why can it help a child wrapped in memo? A stable callback prop can let that child receive equal props and skip a re-render when other relevant props are unchanged.

interview.question: How should the dependency list be chosen?
interview.answer: The dependency list must include every value from the component used by the callback. React compares those dependencies with the previous render using Object.is.
interview.followUp: What if a dependency is omitted? The callback can retain a stale value, so the dependency list should represent all values the function reads.

interview.question: Where may useCallback be called?
interview.answer: useCallback must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook. It cannot be placed in a loop or conditional because Hooks must be called consistently across renders.
interview.followUp: How can conditional behavior be implemented instead? Keep the Hook call unconditional and put the condition inside the callback or split the logic into separate components or Hooks.

keyPoints: It preserves a function definition across renders rather than caching the result of calling that function.
Place the call directly in the component body or in a custom Hook, not inside nested control flow.
The first argument is the callback whose identity React may reuse.
List every reactive component value read by the callback so React knows when its identity must be refreshed.
Unchanged dependencies yield the previous function identity, which is useful for optimized consumers and dependent Hooks.
gotchas: Do not call it inside loops or conditions; invoke it only at the component or custom Hook top level.
Provide both the function definition and its dependency list; omitting either argument is not the documented usage.
A cached identity is conditional, not permanent: changing any dependency produces a different returned function.

Performance hooks::useCallback and memo.summary: useCallback caches a function reference between renders. Pair it with memoized children when stable callback identity lets them skip measured rendering work.
Performance hooks::useCallback and memo.explanation: useCallback caches a function definition between renders and returns the cached function until a dependency changes. This matters when passing a callback to a memoized child: stable callback identity can let memo skip that child’s render when its other props are unchanged.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: The function definition to cache; React returns a cached reference rather than calling it.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline constant dependency array containing every reactive value used by fn.

Performance hooks::useCallback and memo.returns: The function passed as fn, cached until a dependency changes.

example.title: Stable callback for a memoized child
example.explanation: The memoized child can skip work when the parent changes theme because useCallback preserves the onSubmit reference while its dependencies stay unchanged.

useCases.title: Prevent avoidable child work
useCases.scenario: A parent re-renders for unrelated state, while a memoized child receives a callback prop.

useCases.title: Stabilize a Hook dependency
useCases.scenario: A callback is read by another Hook’s dependency list.

useCases.title: Control function identity
useCases.scenario: A callback captures changing props or state but should remain stable between those changes.

interview.question: What does useCallback do, and when does the cached function change?
interview.answer: useCallback returns a cached function reference. React reuses that reference until one of the listed dependencies changes; the function is not invoked by useCallback.
interview.followUp: Why pair it with memo? memo compares props, so a newly created callback would count as a changed prop; useCallback can keep that prop stable when its captured values are stable.

interview.question: How do useCallback and memo work together?
interview.answer: memo creates a component version that usually skips a parent-caused render when props are unchanged. It is an optimization rather than a guarantee, and it does not prevent renders caused by the component’s own state or context.
interview.followUp: What if the callback is stable but another prop is a new object each render? The child can still render because memo compares that object by reference.

interview.question: How should dependencies be chosen?
interview.answer: The dependency list must include every reactive value used by the callback, including props, state, and values declared in the component. React compares dependencies with Object.is; changing one produces a new callback.
interview.followUp: Can a dependency be omitted to force stability? No: that risks a stale closure; instead restructure the code or use an updater when the documentation’s pattern applies.

keyPoints: It returns the same function reference across renders while its dependencies remain equal.
Invoke it unconditionally at component or custom-Hook top level, never inside a loop, condition, or nested function.
List every reactive value read by the callback so it is recreated when captured data changes.
Unlike useMemo, it does not call the supplied function; it caches that function for later invocation.
The useful pairing is a stable callback passed as a prop to a memoized child.
gotchas: Caching a function is only useful when it lets a memoized child skip re-rendering, or when the function is used as a dependency of another Hook.
With React Compiler, you might not need useCallback anymore.

Performance hooks::useMemo.summary: Cache a calculation result between re-renders when dependencies remain unchanged. Use it as a measured performance optimization for expensive pure calculations, not as a correctness mechanism.
Performance hooks::useMemo.explanation: useMemo runs a pure, argument-free calculation during the initial render, then returns its previous result on later renders when every dependency is unchanged by Object.is. If a dependency changes, React recalculates the value. Call it at the top level and use it for measured performance optimization, not side effects.

parameters.name: calculateValue
parameters.description: A pure, argument-free function that calculates and returns the value to cache.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline array with a constant number of items containing all reactive values used by calculateValue.

Performance hooks::useMemo.returns: The cached calculation result, or a newly calculated result when dependencies change.

example.title: Cache a filtered list
example.explanation: Caches the filtered list until either the todo data or search query changes.

useCases.title: Skip expensive recalculations
useCases.scenario: A component re-renders frequently while an expensive pure calculation depends on stable inputs.

useCases.title: Preserve value identity
useCases.scenario: A memoized value is passed to a memoized child and should retain identity while its inputs are unchanged.

useCases.title: Memoize derived data
useCases.scenario: A derived list or value depends on props or state and should update only when those reactive inputs change.

interview.question: How does useMemo decide whether to recalculate?
interview.answer: useMemo caches a calculation result between renders. React compares the dependency list with the previous list using Object.is; unchanged dependencies reuse the cached value, while a changed dependency causes recalculation.
interview.followUp: What must the calculation function be like? It must be pure, take no arguments, and return the value to cache; it runs during rendering, so it must not perform side effects.

interview.question: What belongs in useMemo's dependency list?
interview.answer: Pass a calculation function and an inline dependency array containing every reactive value used by that function. The array must have a constant number of items.
interview.followUp: What happens if a dependency is omitted? The calculation can observe stale data, so every referenced reactive value should be included.

interview.question: When should useMemo be used?
interview.answer: useMemo is intended to skip expensive recalculations caused by re-renders. It does not make the initial render faster, and it should be added when measurement shows that the calculation is costly.
interview.followUp: Can correctness rely on the cache? No. Memoization is an optimization; code must remain correct if React removes the cached value.

keyPoints: useMemo stores a calculation result so later renders can reuse it instead of repeating the same work.
The calculation runs on the first render, so useMemo cannot reduce the initial cost.
React reuses the cached result only when each dependency remains Object.is-equal to its previous value.
Changing any dependency invalidates the old result and causes the calculation to run again.
The first argument is the function that produces the value; it receives no arguments and should be pure.
The dependency array should list every reactive value referenced by the calculation.
gotchas: It is a Hook, so call useMemo only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; never place it in a loop or condition.
Keep the dependency array inline with a constant length and include every reactive value referenced by the calculation.

Performance hooks::useMemo and the React.summary: useMemo caches a pure calculation between renders until its dependencies change. React Compiler can memoize automatically, so manual useMemo is usually unnecessary in new code unless precise control is needed.
Performance hooks::useMemo and the React.explanation: useMemo caches a pure, argument-free calculation between renders and recalculates it when any listed dependency changes. React Compiler can perform memoization automatically, so new code should generally rely on the compiler and retain useMemo only when explicit control is useful.

parameters.name: calculateValue
parameters.description: A pure, argument-free function that computes the value to cache.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline dependency array with a constant length, containing every component value used by the calculation.

example.title: Memoize a derived list
example.explanation: This component caches filtering until products or query changes. With the React Compiler enabled, prefer removing this manual memoization unless precise control is needed.

useCases.title: Cache expensive calculations
useCases.scenario: A component performs an expensive pure transformation of props or state and should reuse the result while its inputs are unchanged.

useCases.title: Control value identity
useCases.scenario: A value is intentionally stabilized for another Hook or API that observes dependency identity.

useCases.title: Apply targeted manual control
useCases.scenario: The compiler cannot or should not determine the exact memoization boundary required by a component.

interview.question: What does useMemo do?
interview.answer: useMemo stores a calculation result between renders. React returns the stored value while dependencies remain unchanged, and calls the calculation again after a dependency changes.
interview.followUp: Why can the compiler reduce manual useMemo? It analyzes React code at build time and can automatically memoize values and functions.

interview.question: What arguments does useMemo require?
interview.answer: Pass a function with no arguments and a dependency list containing every component value used by that function. React compares dependencies with Object.is to decide whether to reuse the cached result.
interview.followUp: What restriction applies to the dependency list? It must contain a constant number of items and be written inline.

interview.question: When is manual useMemo unnecessary?
interview.answer: React Compiler automatically memoizes values and functions, reducing the need for manual useMemo calls. For new code, rely on the compiler by default and use useMemo when precise control is needed.
interview.followUp: Can useMemo remain in a compiler-enabled application? Yes; the documentation describes it as an escape hatch for controlling which values are memoized.

keyPoints: useMemo caches a derived calculation so repeated renders can reuse its previous result.
An unchanged dependency list lets React return the cached value instead of recalculating.
Dependency comparisons use Object.is semantics, so a changed reference can invalidate the cache.
When the React Compiler is enabled, automatic memoization commonly removes the need to write useMemo by hand.
Manual useMemo remains available when a component needs deliberate control over memoization.
gotchas: Call useMemo only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; do not place it in loops or conditions.
Keep the dependency list inline and fixed in length; include every value read by the calculation.
The calculation must be pure and argument-free; useMemo is not a substitute for managing side effects.

Performance hooks::useMemo cache semanti.summary: useMemo caches a calculation result between re-renders when its dependencies are unchanged. Treat it only as a performance optimization, never as storage for required application state.
Performance hooks::useMemo cache semanti.explanation: `useMemo` stores the result of a pure, argument-free calculation between renders. React compares the dependency list with the previous one using `Object.is`; unchanged dependencies reuse the prior result, while changed dependencies trigger recalculation. The cached value is not guaranteed storage, so required correctness must not depend on it.

parameters.name: calculateValue
parameters.description: A pure calculation function with no arguments that returns the value to cache.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline list of all reactive values used by the calculation.

Performance hooks::useMemo cache semanti.returns: The cached calculation result, reused while dependencies remain unchanged; otherwise the newly calculated result.

example.explanation: The filtered array is recalculated only when `todos` or `filter` changes; the calculation remains a pure render-time optimization.

useCases.title: Skip expensive recalculations
useCases.scenario: An expensive pure transformation of props or state is repeated on renders with unchanged inputs.

useCases.title: Stabilize derived props
useCases.scenario: A derived object or array must retain a stable identity so an optimized child can skip an avoidable re-render.

useCases.title: Reduce update-time work
useCases.scenario: A render-time calculation is pure but costly during updates.

interview.question: When does `useMemo` reuse its value?
interview.answer: `useMemo` caches a calculation result between renders. React reuses that result when every dependency is unchanged according to `Object.is`; otherwise it runs the calculation again.
interview.followUp: What if the cached value is needed for correctness? That indicates a design problem: use state or another appropriate mechanism, because React can discard a memoized value.

interview.question: What belongs in the dependency list?
interview.answer: Pass a calculation function with no arguments and a dependency list containing every value used by that calculation. Missing dependencies can leave the calculation based on stale inputs.
interview.followUp: Why must the calculation be pure? It executes during rendering, and render-time side effects can run unexpectedly or be repeated.

interview.question: When should a component use `useMemo`?
interview.answer: `useMemo` is an optimization for avoiding unnecessary recalculation, especially on updates. It does not make the initial render faster and should not be used as application-state storage.
interview.followUp: How should performance work be targeted? Verify that the calculation or interaction is actually slow, then memoize the measured bottleneck.

keyPoints: It memoizes a calculation's returned value across renders.
The first argument is a zero-argument calculation callback.
List every reactive value read by the calculation as a dependency.
Unchanged dependencies let React reuse the previous result.
Any changed dependency causes recalculation and replacement of the memoized result.
The technique is memoization: caching outputs associated with inputs.
gotchas: Do not use the cached value as required application state; fix code that fails when memoization is absent.
The cache is not a semantic guarantee, so code must tolerate React discarding it.
It helps skip work on updates, not initial rendering.

Ref hooks::useImperativeHandle.summary: useImperativeHandle customizes the value exposed through a ref. Use it to give a parent a small imperative API instead of exposing the child’s DOM node or implementation.
Ref hooks::useImperativeHandle.explanation: Call this Hook at the component’s top level with the received ref and a factory that returns the limited handle the parent may use. Keep the actual DOM node in a separate ref; React recreates the handle when listed reactive dependencies change, while an empty dependency list preserves the same handle when its factory reads no reactive values.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The ref received as a prop by the component; this is the ref whose exposed value will be customized.

parameters.name: createHandle
parameters.description: A no-argument function returning the handle to expose. The handle may have any type, commonly an object of methods.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline array containing every reactive value used by createHandle; it must have a constant length.

example.title: Expose a narrow input API
example.explanation: The component keeps the DOM ref private and exposes only focus and clear methods to its parent.

useCases.title: Encapsulated input controls
useCases.scenario: A parent needs to focus or clear a child input without directly accessing its DOM node.

useCases.title: Narrow component APIs
useCases.scenario: A child exposes a small set of imperative methods while keeping internal DOM references private.

useCases.title: Exceptional imperative actions
useCases.scenario: An interaction cannot be expressed conveniently with props and state alone.

interview.question: What problem does useImperativeHandle solve?
interview.answer: useImperativeHandle customizes the value exposed through a ref. Its factory returns the handle, which may be any type but is commonly an object containing only the methods the parent needs.
interview.followUp: How do you avoid exposing the entire input DOM node? Keep the DOM node in a separate useRef and pass the parent’s ref to useImperativeHandle with selected methods.

interview.question: What are the arguments to useImperativeHandle?
interview.answer: The first argument is the ref received by the component, and the second is a no-argument factory that returns the exposed handle. The optional dependency list contains every reactive value referenced by that factory.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the factory reads state? Include that state in the dependency list so React can recreate the handle when the value changes.

interview.question: How is useImperativeHandle used in React 19?
interview.answer: In React 19, a function component can receive ref as a prop and pass it directly to useImperativeHandle. The Hook itself returns undefined, and the parent reads the resulting handle from its ref.
interview.followUp: When should this Hook be avoided? Prefer ordinary props and declarative state; use an imperative handle only for a small imperative API that cannot be expressed declaratively.

keyPoints: It replaces the default ref value with a custom handle chosen by the child component.
A method-only object lets the parent perform specific imperative actions without receiving the child’s implementation details.
The exposed handle is not limited to objects; the factory may return any suitable value.
Dependencies cover props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component that the factory uses.
Write dependencies inline and keep their count stable across renders.
gotchas: Hooks must be called at the component’s top level, not conditionally or inside nested functions.
Dependencies must remain an inline array with a fixed length.
Do not use the Hook’s return value; it configures the supplied ref instead.

Ref hooks::useImperativeHandle dependenc.summary: useImperativeHandle accepts an optional dependency list for the values used by createHandle. React recreates and reassigns the exposed handle when a dependency changes, or after every re-render when the list is omitted.
Ref hooks::useImperativeHandle dependenc.explanation: The optional dependency list describes every reactive value read by createHandle, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component. React compares dependencies with Object.is; if one changes, createHandle runs again and its new result is assigned to the ref. The list must have a constant length and be written inline.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The ref received by the component; the handle created by createHandle is exposed through it.

parameters.name: createHandle
parameters.description: A no-argument function that returns the handle to expose. The handle may have any type; an object of methods is usual.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline list of all reactive values referenced by createHandle. Its length must remain constant.

example.title: Recreate a handle when its reactive dependency changes
example.explanation: The exposed handle is recreated when the reactive value used by createHandle, text, changes.

useCases.title: Expose selected methods
useCases.scenario: A component exposes a small imperative API, such as focus or text retrieval, instead of its whole DOM node.

useCases.title: Refresh a stateful handle
useCases.scenario: A handle method closes over changing state or props and must reflect their latest values.

useCases.title: Keep a stable handle
useCases.scenario: A handle is independent of reactive values and should remain stable across renders.

interview.question: What belongs in useImperativeHandle's dependency list?
interview.answer: The list contains all reactive values referenced inside createHandle. This includes props, state, and variables or functions declared directly in the component; React compares each dependency with its previous value using Object.is.
interview.followUp: What happens without the list? createHandle re-executes on every re-render and the newly created handle is assigned to the ref.

interview.question: When is the exposed handle recreated?
interview.answer: React recreates the exposed handle when a dependency changes according to Object.is. It then assigns the newly created handle to the ref.
interview.followUp: Why must the list be inline? Its item count must remain constant so React can compare corresponding dependencies between renders.

interview.question: What does useImperativeHandle return, and what does createHandle return?
interview.answer: useImperativeHandle returns undefined. Its purpose is to customize the handle exposed through the supplied ref, while createHandle returns the handle value itself.
interview.followUp: What can the returned handle contain? Any type is allowed, although the documentation says an object containing the intended methods is usual.

keyPoints: List every reactive value read by createHandle, not only state variables; props and component-local declarations also count.
Props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component body are reactive values.
React uses Object.is to decide whether each dependency changed.
A changed dependency triggers createHandle to produce a new exposed handle.
After recreation, React assigns the new handle to the ref.
gotchas: Keep the dependency list inline and constant in length; dynamically constructing it is not supported.
Omitting dependencies causes createHandle to run after every re-render, rather than only when selected values change.

Ref hooks::useRef.summary: useRef creates a stable ref object for storing a mutable value or referring to a DOM node without causing a re-render when current changes.
Ref hooks::useRef.explanation: Call useRef with an initial value to obtain a stable object whose mutable current property can hold a value or a DOM node. React preserves that object between renders, changing current does not trigger a render, and passing the object to a JSX ref attribute lets React assign the associated DOM node.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: The value assigned to the ref object's current property initially; it may be any type and is ignored after the first render.

Ref hooks::useRef.returns: An object with a single mutable current property, initially set to initialValue. React can populate current with a JSX node when the object is passed as its ref attribute; the same object is returned on subsequent renders.

example.title: Focus a DOM element with a ref
example.explanation: The ref stores the input DOM node, and the click handler uses it to focus the input without requiring state or an extra render.

useCases.title: Retain non-rendering data
useCases.scenario: Store a timeout ID or another mutable value that must survive renders without affecting displayed output.

useCases.title: Access a DOM node
useCases.scenario: Keep a reference to an input, container, or other JSX node for browser API calls.

useCases.title: Bridge to external APIs
useCases.scenario: Coordinate with browser APIs or other non-React systems using an imperative handle.

interview.question: What does useRef return, and what happens when current changes?
interview.answer: useRef returns an object with one current property. React keeps the same object on later renders, while changing current is mutable and does not cause the component to render again.
interview.followUp: How would you choose between useRef and useState? Use state when a change affects rendered output; use a ref when the value is needed across renders but does not belong in the visual result.

interview.question: How do you use useRef to access a DOM node?
interview.answer: Pass an initial value to useRef at the top level of a component, then access or assign the stored value through ref.current. For a DOM ref, pass that object to a JSX node's ref attribute and React assigns the node after rendering.
interview.followUp: What is the initial DOM-ref value? Usually null, because the node does not exist during the initial render; code should account for current being null.

interview.question: What is the purpose of useRef's argument?
interview.answer: The argument supplies the ref object's initial current value and may have any type. React ignores that argument after the initial render, so it is not a reset mechanism.
interview.followUp: Why should the initial value match the intended use? A DOM ref commonly starts as null, while a stored timer identifier or mutable value should start with an appropriate value for its type.

keyPoints: Use it for information that does not determine the component's rendered output.
Invoke it at the component's top level rather than conditionally or inside another function.
The current property is intentionally mutable, so event-driven code can replace the stored value.
A JSX ref attribute connects the object to the corresponding rendered node.
The ref object's identity remains stable across renders, making it suitable for retaining values.
A ref can hold arbitrary data, including identifiers, objects, or DOM nodes.
gotchas: Do not use a ref for data that must immediately change what the component displays; use state for that instead.
Read or update current in event handlers or other non-rendering code, not during the component's render.
The initial value is not reapplied on later renders, so changing the argument does not reset the ref.

Ref hooks::useRef instance values.summary: useRef stores a mutable value in a stable ref object that React retains between renders. Updating ref.current does not trigger a re-render, making it useful for timers, previous values, and imperative handles that do not affect the UI.
Ref hooks::useRef instance values.explanation: useRef creates a stable ref object whose mutable current property can hold information that is not needed for rendering. React retains the object across renders, but changing current does not schedule a render, so use state when the value must affect visible output.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: The initial value for the ref object's current property; it may be any type.

Ref hooks::useRef instance values.returns: A stable ref object with a mutable current property.

example.title: Store a timer handle
example.explanation: The ref retains the interval handle between renders without causing renders when its current value changes.

useCases.title: Previous values
useCases.scenario: Keep a prior prop or state value for comparison in an effect or event handler.

useCases.title: Imperative handles
useCases.scenario: Hold a mutable integration handle for a browser API or another non-React system.

interview.question: What does useRef return, and how does it differ from state?
interview.answer: useRef returns a plain object with a current property. React keeps the same object between renders, and updating current does not trigger a re-render.
interview.followUp: How would you store a value that must update the displayed UI? Use state, because React schedules a re-render when its setter updates the value.

interview.question: How is a ref initialized and updated?
interview.answer: Pass the initial value as the hook's only argument. The ref starts with that value in current, and later assignments can replace it.
interview.followUp: What should the initial value be for a timer handle? Use a value such as null, then assign the handle after the timer is created.

interview.question: When is a ref preferable to state?
interview.answer: Use a ref for information that is not required for rendering, such as a timeout ID or another mutable handle. It persists across renders without making each update render the component.
interview.followUp: Why should ref.current not appear as an Effect dependency? Its mutation is not reactive, so React cannot know when to re-run the Effect.

keyPoints: Call the hook in the component and supply the starting value for current.
Read or replace the stored value through the ref's current property.
A ref remains available after the component renders again, making it suitable for previous values and handles.
Assigning current is not a rendering mechanism; it leaves the UI unchanged unless some other update occurs.
Conceptually, the returned ref is a simple object containing one mutable slot.
gotchas: Avoid reading or assigning current while rendering; perform those operations in event handlers or effects.
A ref is the wrong choice for data that determines the rendered result; use state so React can update the screen.
Mutability is deliberate, but changing current alone does not notify React or refresh the component.

State hooks::useReducer.summary: `useReducer` manages component state through a pure reducer and dispatched actions. It returns the current state and a dispatch function that triggers updates.
State hooks::useReducer.explanation: `useReducer` returns state plus a dispatch function. Dispatch sends an action to a pure reducer, which receives the current state and action and returns the next state; an optional initializer can calculate the initial state from `initialArg`.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Pure function receiving the current state and action, then returning the next state.

parameters.name: initialArg
parameters.description: Value used to calculate the initial state.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Optional initializer called as init(initialArg) to produce the initial state.

State hooks::useReducer.returns: An array with exactly two values: the current state and a dispatch function.

example.explanation: The component dispatches an action, and the pure reducer calculates the next state.

useCases.title: Centralize complex transitions
useCases.scenario: Several related values change together in response to named events.

useCases.title: Keep handlers concise
useCases.scenario: Many event handlers contain similar state-update logic.

useCases.title: Use lazy initialization
useCases.scenario: Initial state requires calculation from input data.

useCases.title: Test a pure reducer
useCases.scenario: A component’s state logic should be easier to test independently.

interview.question: What does `useReducer` return and how does dispatch work?
interview.answer: `useReducer` returns an array containing the current state and a dispatch function. Dispatching an action requests a state update and a re-render, while the reducer computes the next state from the current state and action.
interview.followUp: How is the initial state established? Without `init`, React uses `initialArg`; with `init`, it uses `init(initialArg)`.

interview.question: What rules must a reducer follow?
interview.answer: The reducer must be pure, accept state and action, and return the next state. Actions can be any type, though object actions commonly describe what the user did.
interview.followUp: Why use an initializer? It moves initial-state calculation into `init(initialArg)`, avoiding repeated calculation during later renders.

interview.question: Where may `useReducer` be called?
interview.answer: Hooks must be called at the top level of a component or custom Hook, so `useReducer` cannot be conditional or inside a loop. This preserves a stable Hook call order across renders.
interview.followUp: What should happen when an action is unknown? The reducer should preserve the current state rather than accidentally returning an unrelated value.

keyPoints: Use it when a component’s state transitions are best centralized in a reducer.
Invoke it at component top level and destructure the returned state and dispatch function.
The reducer maps the current state and an action to the next state without side effects.
Event handlers update the UI by dispatching an action that describes the user’s operation.
The first returned value is the state used for the current render.
The second returned value is dispatch, which requests a different state and another render.
Omitting `init` makes `initialArg` the initial state directly.
gotchas: Call the Hook only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; do not place it in loops or conditions.
In Strict Mode during development, React may call the reducer and initializer twice to help detect accidental impurities; keep both pure.

State hooks::useReducer lazy initializat.summary: Use useReducer's optional third argument to derive initial state from initialArg through init. React performs that initialization once; reset deliberately by dispatching an action that derives the desired starting state again.
State hooks::useReducer lazy initializat.explanation: Pass the initial input as the second argument and an initializer as the third. React uses init(initialArg) for the first state, then retains that state on later renders; a reducer action can deliberately call the same initialization logic to reset state.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Reducer function that receives the current state and dispatched action and returns the next state.

parameters.name: initialArg
parameters.description: Input from which the initial state is calculated; it may be any value.

parameters.name: init
parameters.description: Optional function that returns the initial state from initialArg.

State hooks::useReducer lazy initializat.returns: An array containing the current state and a dispatch function. During the first render, the state is init(initialArg), or initialArg when init is omitted.

example.title: Lazy initialization with a reset action
example.explanation: The third argument supplies the initializer, while the reset action explicitly derives a fresh state from the same initial input.

useCases.title: Derive state from an input
useCases.scenario: Initial state depends on props, persisted data, or another input that must be transformed before use.

useCases.title: Avoid repeated setup
useCases.scenario: Initialization performs nontrivial state construction that should not be repeated on ordinary renders.

useCases.title: Implement explicit reset
useCases.scenario: A form, wizard, or editor needs a reducer-managed reset to a known baseline.

interview.question: How does lazy initialization determine the first state?
interview.answer: The signature is useReducer(reducer, initialArg, init?). With init, the first state is init(initialArg); without it, the first state is initialArg.
interview.followUp: Why use the third argument? It lets initialization be expressed as a function receiving an input, rather than constructing the derived state directly in the component.

interview.question: What happens if initialArg changes after mount?
interview.answer: React retains the initial state after initialization and does not recalculate it on ordinary later renders. A changing initialArg therefore does not reset the reducer automatically.
interview.followUp: How would you reset predictably? Add a reset action whose reducer branch returns state derived from the desired initial input, or remount with a changed key when that behavior is intended.

interview.question: How should a reset action reuse lazy initialization?
interview.answer: The initializer is passed as a function reference, such as init, not as init(initialArg). The reducer can reuse that function in a reset branch to derive the reset state from the same input.
interview.followUp: What if initialization has no input? Pass null as initialArg and let init create the initial state.

keyPoints: The third argument is an optional initializer function, and it must return the initial reducer state.
When init is supplied, React computes the first state by calling it with initialArg.
The initial state comes from init(initialArg), or directly from initialArg when no initializer is provided.
Supplying an initializer avoids recreating derived initial state on subsequent renders.
gotchas: Changing the initial argument on a later render does not reset the reducer. Handle reset explicitly in the reducer, or use a different component key when a remount is appropriate.

State hooks::useState functional updates.summary: Use a functional updater when the next state depends on pending state. React queues pure updater functions and applies them in order during the next render, so multiple dependent updates are handled correctly.
State hooks::useState functional updates.explanation: A state setter accepts either a replacement value or a pure updater function. The updater receives the pending state, returns the next state, and is queued; React applies queued updaters in order during the next render, making this form reliable when several updates depend on one another.

parameters.name: nextState
parameters.description: The replacement state, or a pure updater function receiving pending state and returning the next state.

State hooks::useState functional updates.returns: The `useState` Hook returns the current state and a setter function that updates it for the next render.

example.title: Queue dependent updates
example.explanation: Each updater receives the latest queued count, so one click increases the value by three.

useCases.title: Compose multiple dependent updates
useCases.scenario: Several clicks or actions update one state variable before React renders again.

useCases.title: Derive state safely
useCases.scenario: An update must derive a list, object, or counter from its current pending value.

useCases.title: Avoid unnecessary Effect dependencies
useCases.scenario: An Effect updates state without reading that state as a dependency.

related: queueing a series of state updates

interview.question: When should you use a functional state update?
interview.answer: Pass a function such as `setAge(a => a + 1)` when the next value depends on the current or pending value. React queues that updater and applies it during the next render.
interview.followUp: Why can three direct `setAge(age + 1)` calls produce only one increment? They all calculate from the same render snapshot; updater functions instead receive each preceding queued result.

interview.question: How does React process multiple updater functions?
interview.answer: React treats a function passed to the setter as an updater, places it in a queue, and applies queued updaters in order. Each updater receives the result produced by the preceding updater.
interview.followUp: What property must those functions have? They must be pure and return only the calculated next state.

interview.question: What does the updater-function argument represent?
interview.answer: The setter schedules the state change for the next render, rather than mutating the state value held by the current render. The updater's argument is the pending state React is processing.
interview.followUp: What naming convention is common for the argument? Use the first letter of the state variable, such as `a` for `age`, or a clearer name like `prevAge`.

keyPoints: A setter can receive either a replacement value or a function that derives the next value from prior state.
A function supplied as the setter argument is interpreted as an updater rather than stored as state.
React queues the updater and schedules a render instead of applying it as an immediate mutation.
During the next render, React derives state by applying every queued updater to the previous state.
The updater receives pending state and computes the value that should replace it.
Queued updater functions execute in submission order, so dependent updates compose predictably.
gotchas: Keep updater functions pure: accept only the pending state and return the next state without side effects.
Do not expect the current render's state variable to change immediately after calling the setter.

State hooks::useState lazy initializatio.summary: Compute an expensive initial state once by passing a pure initializer function to useState. React calls it during initialization, stores its return value, and ignores the initial-state argument on later renders.
State hooks::useState lazy initializatio.explanation: Pass a pure, zero-argument function to useState when calculating the initial value is expensive. React invokes it during initialization, stores the returned value as state, and ignores the initial-state argument on later renders.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: The initial state value, or a pure zero-argument initializer function whose return value becomes the initial state.

State hooks::useState lazy initializatio.returns: An array containing the current state and a set function that updates the state and triggers a re-render.

example.title: Initialize an expensive todo list once
example.explanation: Pass the initializer function itself, without calling it, so React uses its returned value for the initial state.

useCases.title: Build an initial list or map only when the component initializes.
useCases.scenario: Large default collections

useCases.title: Parse or transform a costly initial data structure without repeating the work on re-renders.
useCases.scenario: Expensive parsing

useCases.title: Read and convert an initial value from a browser-provided source when the component starts.
